Trump administration to invest $3 billion in minerals projects to boost US defence supply chains. The US government will invest $3 billion in critical minerals and battery projects as part of a push to increase domestic production and boost national security and industrial policy, US President Donald Trump said on Friday. “We’re reclaiming America’s rightful place as the minerals superpower of the world,” Trump told more than 200 mining executives, educators, investors and fellow politicians at a roundtable at the State Department aimed at supporting the industry, which he said had not received enough attention from Washington in recent years. He announced a slew of investments during his speech, including a $1.4bn conditional loan from the Defence Department’s Office of Strategic Capital for Sila Nanotechnologies, which makes lithium-ion battery parts. The OSC also extended a $400 million conditional loan to scandium miner Sunrise Energy Metals and a $150m conditional loan to magnet developer Niron Magnetics. The US Export-Import Bank will lend $58m to Westwater Resources, Global Advanced Metals and 5E Advanced Materials, which Reuters reported earlier on Friday. “Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA,” Trump said. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and National Security Council official David Copley attended the announcement. Weapons stockpiles drive mineral demand The White House needs critical minerals to replenish weapons stockpiles depleted during the Iran conflict and reduce US dependence on Chinese supply chains. Several executives came with gifts for Trump. Tom Albanese, chairman of deep-sea mining firm American Ocean Minerals, gave Trump a gold replica of a nodule that the company hopes to mine from the Pacific seabed. Trump last year said he may bypass the UN-backed International Seabed Authority and issue international seabed mining licenses. Jim Litinsky, CEO of rare earths firm MP Materials, which is financially supported by the Pentagon, gave Trump magnets that had been produced for General Motors in the company’s Texas plant. Other attendees included executives from Lithium Americas , which is building the largest US lithium mine, NioCorp, which is building a scandium mine to supply defence contractor Lockheed Martin, and Energy Fuels , which received a $725m OSC conditional loan in June. US forces have burned through large numbers of precision-guided missiles and air-defence interceptors during the five-month-old US- Iran war. Defence officials and lawmakers have warned that replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints. The Trump administration has disputed reports of significant shortages. Supplies of minerals including rare earths, tungsten, germanium and scandium are essential for manufacturing precision-guided missiles, fighter aircraft, armored vehicles, infrared sensors and other advanced weapons systems, according to Pentagon officials and defence companies. Mining schools receive funding boost The Department of Energy on Friday hosted representatives from all 14 accredited US mining schools to promote mining careers and encourage more students to enter the field. The department announced $100m in grants to help boost educational programs and set a goal of doubling the number of mining-related graduates at the nation’s universities within two years. “We need to work on some systemic changes to how we as a nation want to offer our brightest students an opportunity to participate in this industry,” said Assistant Energy Secretary Audrey Robertson. The Pentagon also said it would fund $80m in projects at three US mining schools. Officials have pointed to China’s extensive network of mining universities as a key advantage in its dominance of global mineral production. Since returning to office, Trump has launched a $12bn strategic minerals stockpile , backed equity investments in companies developing US mines and processing facilities, and sought to limit defence contractors’ reliance on supplies from China. The administration says government support is needed to counter decades of Chinese investment that left Beijing dominant in the mining and processing of many strategic minerals. Australia’s government on Saturday welcomed the Trump administration’s loan to Sunrise Energy Metals, which is developing a scandium mine in the country’s New South Wales state. “The Sunrise Scandium Project hosts the world’s largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications,” Resources Minister Madeleine King said in a statement.

Captain martyred, 7 terrorists killed in intelligence-based operation in Hangu: ISPR. The military’s media affairs wing said on Saturday that a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Hangu district. In a statement , Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said security forces conducted an IBO in Hangu on Friday following reports about the presence of terrorists belonging to Fitna al Khawarij — a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. During the operation, troops effectively engaged the terrorists, it said. “In desperation, the khawarij took refuge inside a mosque, blatantly disregarding the sanctity of the place of worship. In ensuing fire exchange, seven khawarij belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khawarij were sent to hell,” it said. The statement went on to say that during the exchange of fire, 27-year-old Captain Hamza Akram, a resident of Punjab’s Narowal district who was “leading his troops from front and relentlessly pursuing” the terrorists, embraced martyrdom. “Weapons and ammunition were also recovered from the killed khawarij , who remained actively involved in numerous terrorist activities against the security forces and law enforcement agencies as well as killing of innocent civilians,” it said. ISPR said that a sanitisation operation was being conducted to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored terrorists in the area. President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to the martyred captain, saying, “The motherland pays its profound tribute to the great sacrifice of its brave son.” “The entire nation is indebted to the eternal sacrifices of these brave sons for the motherland,” the president added, offering prayers for the bereaved family. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over Captain Akram’s martyrdom while hailing his courage and devotion, state-run APP reported. In a statement issued by his office, PM Shehbaz lauded the security forces for eliminating seven terrorists “operating under the Indian patronage”. “The nation will never forget the sacrifices of its brave sons,” the press release quoted him as saying. He prayed for the captain’s elevated ranks and for patience for his family. The prime minister reiterated that operations against Fitna al Khawarij would continue till complete elimination of terrorism. “The sacrifices rendered by our brave armed forces and law-enforcement agencies for the defence, peace and security of the country and nation will not go in vain,” he asserted. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also paid tribute to the martyred captain and offered his condolences to the bereaved family. He said that the officer had paid the ultimate sacrifice for the homeland and would remain alive in our hearts. A day earlier, ISPR said 10 terrorists were killed in two separate engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It said that in the first encounter, a group of terrorists attempted to attack security forces’ checkposts in Azam Warsak area in South Waziristan, which was effectively thwarted, resulting in the deaths of eight terrorists. “In another encounter that took place in Dir district, own troops successfully neutralised two more khawarij ,” it added. Terrorist commander killed in Bannu Separately, security forces killed a key terrorist commander, identified as Jamidullah, during an operation in Jani Khel area of KP’s Bannu district, a security official said. The official said that the terrorist commander was involved in terrorist activities and was considered a quadcopter expert. The official said that security forces conducted the operation in Jani Khel on the basis of intelligence reports, during which Jamidullah was targeted and killed. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , an Islamabad-based think tank, violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed.

Heavy rain disrupts traffic, daily life in Lahore’s low-lying areas. LAHORE: Heavy rain lashed Lahore on Saturday, inundating low-lying areas, major roads and several underpasses, making movement difficult for pedestrians and motorists in different parts of the city. The downpour disrupted normal traffic as rainwater accumulated on roads and in low-lying localities, leaving motorists struggling to navigate waterlogged stretches. Pedestrians also struggled to move through streets and roads where water had accumulated. According to rainfall data from the Water and Sanitation Agency (Wasa), the city received an average of 24.6mm of rain. The highest rainfall of 104mm was recorded at the airport, followed by 75.6mm at Kahna, 62.6mm at Hadiara Defence Road and 58.6mm at Manawan. Tajpura sub-divisional officer’s (SDO) office recorded 40.2mm of rain, while 32.8mm was recorded at the Mughalpura SDO office. Shadipura received 28.4mm, Nishter Town 28mm, Chowk Nakhuda 11mm, Johar Town SDO Office 11mm, while 10.8mm was recorded at the Wasa head office in Gulberg. Upper Mall received 9mm, Samanabad SDO Office 4.4mm, Iqbal Town SDO Office 3.8mm, Saggian 3.8mm, Lakshmi Chowk 3.2mm, Jail Road 2mm, Gulshan-e-Ravi 1.8mm and Farrukhabad 1.4mm, while only trace rainfall was recorded at Pani Wala Talab. Rain was also reported in Farrukhabad, Tajpura, Defence Phase-VI, Shadipura, Saggian, Lakshmi Chowk, Chowk Nakhuda and surrounding areas. Harbanspura and several other localities received heavy showers. The rain brought relief from the heat and made the weather pleasant, but waterlogging in several areas caused inconvenience to residents and exposed the vulnerability of low-lying localities to heavy rainfall. Meanwhile, Wasa Lahore said it had deployed field staff and machinery at various locations to drain accumulated rainwater. Wasa Managing Director Ghufran Ahmed inspected drainage operations at Mubeen Shaheed Underpass, Noor Jehan Road, MM Alam Road, Main Boulevard Gulberg, Qaddafi Stadium and Liberty Chowk. He also visited Kalma Chowk Underpass, Garden Town Water Tank, Usman Block Emergency Relief Camp and Usman Block Disposal Station. Officials said drainage operations were continuing at waterlogged locations, with heavy machinery deployed in low-lying areas. Disposal stations in areas experiencing power outages were being operated on generators. Wasa Vice Chairman Chaudhry Shehbaz Ahmed also inspected drainage operations at Shalimar Link Road, Bhagwanpura, Baghichi Sethan, UET, Ek Moriya, Do Moriya and Chowk Na Khuda. Earlier, Chief Traffic Officer (CTO) Abdul Rahim Shirazi directed supervisory officers to remain in the field and monitor low-lying points and traffic conditions during the rainfall. Traffic officials were directed to coordinate with Wasa for the timely drainage of rainwater from waterlogged locations. Traffic police advised motorists to drive at moderate speeds, maintain a safe distance from other vehicles and avoid sudden braking on slippery roads. Motorcyclists were advised to wear helmets and avoid unnecessary overtaking. Citizens were also advised to assess the depth of accumulated water before entering flooded roads and avoid crossing stretches where water levels were unsafe. The traffic police warned citizens against standing near electric poles, transformers, fallen power lines, trees, weak walls and under-construction structures during rainfall.

Pakistan, New Zealand seek to boost cooperation in agri, education sectors. Pakistan and New Zealand discussed boosting cooperation in various fields, with a special focus on agriculture and education, as the two sides held a Joint Trade Committee (JTC) meeting in Wellington, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Saturday. The third Pakistan-New Zealand JTC meeting and the fifth round of Pakistan-New Zealand Political Consultations were held in Wellington on Thursday, “marking a significant step in deepening bilateral engagement between the two countries”, the FO said. A key outcome of the meetings was the signing of the Education Cooperation Arrangement between Pakistan and New Zealand, which is “expected to significantly deepen collaboration in the education sector”. At the JTC meeting, both sides “deliberated on improving market access and enhancing cooperation in sustainable agriculture, including exploring technical collaboration in wool production and plant protection”, the FO said. The discussions focused on bolstering bilateral trade and investment, with particular emphasis on technology, education and services. Institutional mechanisms to further economic cooperation were also discussed, the statement added. Commerce Secretary Jawad Paul Khawaja represented Pakistan during the JTC meeting, while Grahame Morton, deputy secretary of the Americas and Asia Group at New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, headed the other delegation. Meanwhile, during the political consultations, both sides conducted a comprehensive review of bilateral relations. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments, and agreed to enhance coordination within multilateral forums. Additional Foreign Secretary (Asia Pacific) Ambassador Dr Syed Ali Asad Gillani co-chaired the Pakistani side at the political consultations, while Morton headed the New Zealand delegation. Islamabad and Wellington “explored avenues to strengthen cooperation across a wide spectrum of areas of mutual interest, including high-level exchanges, economic development, science and technology, education, counterterrorism, transnational crime, and people-to-people ties”, the FO said. Ambassador Gillani briefed the New Zealand side on Pakistan’s efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East, as Islamabad remains actively engaged in efforts to defuse the Strait of Hormuz stand-off. Morton “acknowledged Pakistan’s constructive role in the Middle East peace process”, the FO statement said. Gillani also discussed the situation in South Asia, including in India-occupied Kashmir (IoK) and India’s “ continued violations ” of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT). India had unilaterally decided to put the IWT in abeyance in late April 2025 after hostilities flared up between the two neighbours last year. The issue of water has remained a bitter point of contention between the nuclear-armed nations since then, with Islamabad repeatedly raising the issue on international platforms. The overall discussions between Pakistan and New Zealand “provided an opportunity to assess progress in bilateral ties, identify new areas for partnership, and reaffirm the shared commitment to a forward-looking and mutually beneficial relationship”, the FO noted. Pakistan and New Zealand enjoy cordial and friendly relations, with both countries being members of the Commonwealth. Bilateral trade stands at $12 million, with Pakistan’s major exports being textile products, apparel, rice, leather articles and sports goods, according to the FO’s website . Main imports from New Zealand include dairy products, wood pulp, paper, edible oil, wood, iron steel and electrical machinery. Agriculture and education were also among areas of cooperation discussed between the two sides when former military dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf visited Auckland in June 2005. Last month, India and New Zealand signed a free trade deal as they sought to boost exports amid global economic uncertainty made worse by the war in the Middle East.

Rana Sanaullah says PML-N will form govt in AJK with two-thirds majority. Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Saturday that the PML-N would form the government in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) with a two-thirds majority. He made the remarks while addressing a rally in Bagh ahead of the third phase of elections in the region. The third phase was originally slated to be held in the 11 constituencies of Poonch division, but will now only be held in its Bagh and Haveli districts due to law and order concerns. Addressing the rally, Sanaullah said that in the first two phases, the PML-N had secured 24 seats. He said that six more seats were required for a two-thirds majority government. Expressing confidence that the public will vote for his PML-N, the minister asserted that four more seats would be added following the August 10 polls, while five more would be added when polls would be held in the rest of Poonch Division. “The PML-N will form a government with a two-thirds majority. The people of Kashmir have trusted PML-N. They have trusted Mian Nawaz Sharif. They have trusted the development in Punjab,” he said. He urged supporters to show up and cast their votes on Monday to help PML-N secure a victory, promising that a PML-N government would prioritise development projects. He also said that once in power, the PML-N government would meet with members of the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC). The JAAC, which has been demanding the abolishment of 12 seats in the local legislature reserved for refugees from Indian-held Kashmir, has been holding protests in the region for several weeks now. “When this government will be set up, with a two-thirds majority, they will sit with [JAAC] representatives. Their first task will be to resolve this issue.” He said that 99 per cent of JAAC protesters were “our brothers”, adding that they were patriotic Kashmiris and Pakistanis. He added that the remainder were focused on creating divisions within the nation. Sanaullah said India was trying to create misunderstandings between Pakistan and Kashmiris after failing to achieve its objectives through direct confrontation, adding that such attempts would never succeed. He urged cooperation between a future PML-N government and the people of AJK in “exposing and defeating” those divisive elements. “We will defeat them and we will make Kashmir prosperous,” Sanaullah said. He further added that in the past, all large-scale development projects in AJK were only completed when the PML-N was in power in the Centre and in the region. He urged the people of Bagh to go out and vote on Monday, stressing that “all of Bagh should be involved in the government”. He added that PML-N founder Nawaz Sharif would fulfil his promises to the people of AJK by nominating one of the three PML-N candidates in Bagh as the future prime minister of AJK. Sanaullah added that Nawaz has already mentioned that he would sit down with the future AJK prime minister to discuss development projects in the region. Highlighting federal support, Sanaullah said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government had approved a Rs23 billion special package for AJK in 2024 and provided wheat subsidy to facilitate the people. He said the prime minister had also approved five Daanish Schools for AJK, while PML-N intended to take forward the public welfare and development model being pursued in Punjab.

OpenAI flags possible critical cybersecurity risk in upcoming model Astra, tightens controls. OpenAI said on Friday it cannot rule out that its upcoming AI model, Astra, has “critical” cybersecurity capabilities, prompting the startup to pause some internal development and trigger safety protocols. Under OpenAI’s safety guidelines, a model reaches the “critical” threshold if it can autonomously identify and exploit severe, real-world software vulnerabilities, known as zero-day exploits, or execute complex cyberattacks against highly secure targets without human intervention. Here are some details on Astra: This follows an exclusive report by Reuters that OpenAI has discovered more instances in which autonomous agents have escaped containment as the company expands its investigation of the hacking incident at tech firm Hugging Face that drew global attention in July. In the last few weeks, OpenAI , Anthropic and Meta Platforms have disclosed that their AI models broke into other companies’ systems during cybersecurity testing, highlighting how advancing AI capabilities are straining developers’ ability to keep their systems contained. Preliminary evaluations over the past several days, along with outside expert assessments, indicated Astra may be capable of performing increasingly sophisticated cyber tasks autonomously, OpenAI said. “While we continue to benchmark and assess this model, our preliminary evaluations indicate strong enough performance that we cannot rule out ‘critical’ capability level at this time,” the ChatGPT maker said. In response to the preliminary findings, OpenAI said it has scaled up security controls and paused internal activities involving Astra that do not meet its newly strengthened security requirements. Astra’s development will be moved into isolated testing environments with restricted network access and sandboxed execution. CEO Sam Altman said on X that OpenAI is working to make Astra generally available, as the company does “not think it is a good strategy to keep powerful models to a chosen few”. OpenAI also clarified that Astra was not involved in the hack targeting the AI platform Hugging Face. It will partner with government agencies and select AI safety organisations to test the model’s capabilities.

Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan's Okinawa, China shuts ports ahead of landfall. Typhoon Dolphin lashed Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture on Saturday, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings, while China shut ports and halted ferries ahead of the storm’s expected arrival on its east coast. Five elderly people, three of whom fell due to strong winds, suffered non-life-threatening injuries in Okinawa while another person was injured in Kagoshima prefecture, authorities said. Nearly 39,000 buildings were without power in Kagoshima while just over 12,000 were affected in Okinawa. Domestic airlines, ANA and Japan Airlines, cancelled flights to and from Okinawa. The typhoon had maximum sustained winds of 162 kilometres per hour with gusts reaching 216 kph. Okinawa and Amami Island in Kagoshima prefecture are the main areas expected to be affected in Japan. Typhoon expected to make landfall in China In China, where the typhoon is expected to make landfall between late on Sunday and early on Monday, authorities have designated Dolphin as an orange-category typhoon, the second-highest level. Worried about the risk of flooding and landslides, authorities also raised the emergency response level for Dolphin by one notch to level III, the second-lowest level. The typhoon is most likely to make landfall between Zhoushan city in Zhejiang province and Fuding city in Fujian province and is expected to have winds of 38-45 metres per second near its centre, according to China’s National Meteorological Centre. Cars drive along a street during heavy rain in Beijing, China on August 7, 2026. — Reuters China’s National Marine Forecasting Centre on Saturday maintained its highest, red-level warning for waves, forecasting 5-to-8-metre (16-to-26-foot) waves in coastal waters off Zhejiang through Sunday afternoon. Under an orange-level warning, waves in coastal waters off Shanghai and northern Fujian could be 3 to 5.5 metres. On Saturday evening, Chinese authorities issued five weather and disaster warnings, including orange alerts for typhoon, heavy rain, and geological-disaster risks, along with a red alert for mountain torrents. Ports and airports halt operations Rain and strong winds are expected to affect eastern China through August 12, including parts of Shanghai and neighbouring provinces. Some areas could see short bursts of rainfall exceeding 80mm an hour, accompanied by thunderstorms and strong winds. Zhejiang, one of China’s biggest provincial economies and a manufacturing and export hub, raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level and halted port operations. Authorities in eastern and southern China also suspended ferries, halted some construction work and ordered fishing boats back to port. Ningbo Lishe International Airport in Zhejiang said it will suspend all flights on Sunday. Shanghai’s Yangshan port had been cleared of vessels by late on Friday, while some rail services in the Yangtze River Delta will be suspended from Sunday. Beijing authorities have said they are monitoring the typhoon’s path and are preparing flood-control and evacuation plans for the capital. In Taiwan, 78 flights, mostly international, were cancelled because of the typhoon, the government said. Heavy rain was expected in northern parts of the island over the weekend, though authorities had not ordered evacuations as of Saturday. China has ordered that, due to the typhoon, ships passing through the Taiwan Strait must heed its traffic control instruction measures that Taipei denounced as “ridiculous”, saying that Beijing has no right to restrict access to international waters. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and claims the strategic strait. Both Taipei and Washington reject that claim.

Hamas says still ready to go ahead with Gaza plan. Hamas said on Saturday it remained ready to proceed with a US-backed Gaza peace plan and urged pressure on Israel, which insists it did not agree to the latest part of the deal. Hamas informed US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace that it stood by the latest stage of the plan, under which the group would hand over weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing committee in the war-battered territory. “Hamas and other factions have confirmed to mediators their readiness to begin implementing the agreement and move to the second phase, provided it receives Israeli approval and that Israel begins implementing the agreement,” a Hamas official told AFP . “Hamas is urging the US administration to exert pressure on Israel to compel it to abide by the agreement and move to the second phase,” the official said on condition of anonymity. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a tough reelection fight in October and wide opposition from his right-wing base to the Gaza deal, said on Tuesday that Israel had not agreed to the “draft” presented by the Board of Peace. Trump last week hailed as a breakthrough that Hamas had agreed to disarmament under the plan, with the Board of Peace saying Israel would in tandem carry out a phased withdrawal from much of Gaza. Netanyahu met Monday with the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, who backtracked and said Israel would withdraw only after a full disarmament by Hamas. Israel’s military also vowed to keep hitting the Palestinian group. But Israeli attacks in Gaza, while ongoing, appear to have decreased in intensity in recent days. On Saturday, the Nasser hospital in Khan Yunis reported three people injured by Israeli army gunfire. Israel has killed 1,257 Palestinians since October last year, when the two sides agreed to a ceasefire backed by Trump, according to the Palestinian health ministry. The Israeli army has reported five deaths in its ranks during the same period.

JI announces Aug 16 sit-ins in provincial capitals to protest petroleum levy. LAHORE: Jamaat-i-Islami Pakistan (JI) has decided to intensify its campaign against the petroleum levy and inflation, announcing simultaneous sit-ins in all four provincial capitals on August 16 to press the government to withdraw the levy. The decision was taken after extensive deliberations at a special meeting of JI’s central and provincial office-bearers, chaired by party chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman at Mansoora on Saturday. Rehman said the sit-ins would be staged outside the Punjab chief minister’s house in Lahore and the governor houses in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh and Balochistan. Under the plan, the JI and its youth and women’s wings will participate in Independence Day activities on August 14, using the occasion to mobilise people around the party’s vision of a just system. The JI chief added that the previous day’s nationwide protest had given the party’s campaign against the petroleum levy and inflation a new direction and fresh momentum; and that over 510 organised and peaceful protests were held across the country, with people from across Pakistan participating. He said the protests had demonstrated that the JI was “becoming a symbol of national unity”, as people from Chitral, Malakand, Hazara and central Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, among others, had raised their voices against the petroleum levy. The JI chief added that the public had rejected the levy and wanted petrol prices reduced to Rs225 per litre. Rehman accused the ruling elite of pushing ordinary citizens into an unbearable inflationary crisis while refusing to cut their own privileges and expenditures. The party chief also claimed the rulers were “unwilling to give up official aircraft, reduce government vehicle expenses or end perks such as free fuel and electricity”, while students, motorcyclists, workers and farmers were being burdened with indirect taxes on petroleum products. “Even people whose incomes were below the taxable threshold were effectively being taxed through fuel prices,” he added. Rehman said the JI had previously taken to the streets to force the government to negotiate with independent power producers (IPP), after initially refusing to engage with them. He added that negotiations had been held with 17 to 18 IPPs, resulting in some reduction in electricity prices, but the process was subsequently halted. “The unresolved energy crisis and rising prices have fuelled an inflationary storm that is affecting every segment of society, particularly salaried people, the middle class and poor families,” Rehman said. He warned that the public could no longer be left to suffer the consequences of government policies and said the rulers would have to deliver their rights. Rehman also welcomed the recently signed defence agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, describing it as “a positive development for the Muslim world”. He said closer cooperation among Islamic countries could lead to a strong bloc and reduce Pakistan’s and the wider Muslim world’s dependence on external powers. Additionally, he proposed expanding the defence cooperation to include Iran, Qatar, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Indonesia, saying efforts should gradually be made to bring all Muslim countries into such a framework. “Muslim countries should overcome their differences, strengthen mutual cooperation and build collective capacity to face regional and global challenges,” Rehman emphasised. A day prior, several major thoroughfares in Karachi were blocked or affected by traffic disruptions as the JI held sit-ins as part of the nationwide demonstration against the petroleum levy. Responding to the protest, Sindh government spokesperson Sadia Javed said the petroleum levy was a federal matter and questioned why Karachi’s citizens were being “punished” through road closures. “Jamaat-i-Islami is using the protest to score political points instead of serving the public,” she alleged, adding that the party should focus on the performance of its local government representatives to improve conditions for Karachi’s residents.

Initial findings of second post-mortem show multiple injuries on Mir Raza Ali, police surgeon says. The initial findings of the second post-mortem examination of 25-year-old business owner Mir Raza Ali revealed multiple injuries and a congealed black substance in his mouth and throat, Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed said on Saturday. Raza, owner of eatery Wafflix, had gone missing on July 28. The 25-year-old’s body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. His body was exhumed earlier today after the Sindh government restored the original medical board. Dr Summaiya told Dawn that Raza had multiple injuries to his head and face, including fractures to his nasal bone and skull. She said there were also injuries to his right flank and feet. The police surgeon added that a congealed black substance was found in Raza’s mouth and throat. Regarding the bullet wound, she said there was a fractured rib in the back, which was the entry point of the gunshot, while the bullet exited through the front. She further said that DNA samples had been collected and sent to a laboratory, along with samples for chemical analysis and gunshot residue testing. The cause of death, she added, would remain reserved until the laboratory reports were received. ‘Tortured and murdered’ Advocate Jibran Nasir, representing the family of the 25-year-old, alleged on Saturday evening that Raza had been tortured before being murdered, hours after his second post-mortem was conducted, and demanded that the entire investigation team be replaced. Speaking to the media in the evening, Nasir said the initial report of the second post-mortem answered “14 questions” and detailed some of the alleged injuries Raza had sustained before his death. “This was murder following torture — the murder of a happy, ambitious and educated young man from Karachi,” he alleged. “He had an injury on his chin,” the advocate said, adding that Raza’s eye sockets were compressed and that traces of a foreign substance were found. “Samples were taken and sent to a lab to see if there are any chemical traces,” he told reporters. The lawyer also claimed that Raza had wounds to his forehead and a fractured nose, as well as swelling and congealed blood around his lower jaw, consistent with having been punched. “There is a fracture to his temple above his ear, indicating he was struck,” he alleged. “In the tongue area, a congealed black substance was discovered, which is not naturally found in the body. This substance has been taken and sent to a lab to see what he was forced to ingest.” Continuing the description, he also claimed that internal muscles in Raza’s throat were covered in the same black substance, and that a broken hyoid bone and muscle damage suggested that he also was strangled. “Now we come to the firearm injury, where it was earlier said that he was shot in the chest and the bullet exited through his back,” Nasir said. “We have now proven 110 per cent that the bullet entered his back and exited after breaking and fracturing his ribs.” The family’s lawyer also criticised senior police officials, alleging that they “do not want to investigate, but rather humiliate, harass and exhaust the family”. “They are finding months-old recordings and frustrating, emotionally exhausting and humiliating Mir Hussain and Maryam Hussain. Are you investigating or harassing them? They sat them in their offices and told them repeatedly, ‘It’s a suicide, accept it’. Our city’s AIG was saying this,” the advocate claimed further. Nasir added that he and the family had “no faith” in the AIG or the SSP’s investigation team and that they wanted the entire team changed, including senior officers. “If they appoint the same kind of officers, such as those doctors from Jamshoro and Hyderabad, then we will approach the court,” he added. “But have no doubts about it: senior officers spent 10 days with the parents and misguided them into believing it was a suicide,” Nasir alleged. Raza’s father, Mir Hussain, told reporters that he had maintained since July 30 that his son’s death was a brutal murder. “We saw the body and told them [that it was murder], but they kept saying, ‘Suicide, suicide, suicide,’” he said. “Sometimes the SSP would talk to us; the IG would say that the matter had been resolved but there was a problem in the report. “If your entire police station investigates based on post-mortem reports, then how can someone in such a position of responsibility say something like this?” Mir Hussain said it “brought us peace” to learn that their claims that Raza had been attacked before his death were true. “We have said it was murder from the start,” he added. “Why are they hiding the killers?” Speaking to the media earlier today, Nasir said the investigation officer was present when the body was exhumed and examined, while all eight members of the medical team were also present. The deceased’s parents were nearby and, “most importantly”, a judicial magistrate was present as well. The lawyer also contended that “incomplete CCTV footage and out-of-context messages” had been used to fuel rumours and draw hasty conclusions since Raza’s death. While his family is convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, investigators probing the incident continue to build their case around the possibility that he died by suicide. Commenting on the medical board controversy, Nasir expressed concern that the government did not provide any reason for changing the medical board overnight on Friday. The lawyer said the victim’s family did not need “character certificates” for the doctors on the medical board. He expressed hope that the medical board’s report would be received by Saturday evening, which would help clarify the circumstances of the young businessman’s death. The report would clearly indicate if the incident was a murder or suicide, Nasir said, adding that the “police will be under even more pressure” once that question was cleared up. He reiterated that the report would answer the question of whether it was “self-inflicted or a murder”. Nasir further said he was surprised to know that the police had shared audio evidence with the media before revealing it to the parents of the victim, who found out about it from TV reports. Nasir expressed gratitude to the judiciary for intervening in the case, adding that “the work that police could not do in eight to nine days was done in two days after judicial intervention”. Separately, a PPP delegation comprising MPAs Asif Moosa and Saima Agha visited Raza’s family to convey their condolences. Moosa assured the bereaved family that Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar and Sindh Inspector General Javed Alam Odho were monitoring the case. He affirmed that efforts were being made for a transparent inquiry so that justice can be served. Saima said the probe will be taken forward once the post-mortem report is compiled, asserting that the culprits will be punished. She further said the PPP stood with the victim’s family. Medical board controversy The exhumation, which was scheduled for Friday morning, was postponed after the deceased’s family objected to the abrupt reconstitution of the medical board and inclusion of members from outside Karachi division. On Thursday, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Raza’s father, Mir Hussain Ali, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation. The court ruling came after a controversy emerged between the Karachi police surgeon and investigators over alleged loopholes in the medico-legal report regarding the post-mortem examination. Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed, whose assessment was based only on the post-mortem report and photographs as she had not examined the body herself, said some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with Dr Syed as the convener. Prof Dr Naseem Ahmed of Dow University of Health Sciences, Dr Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Amir Hassan Khan of Citizens Police Liaison Committee, Additional Police Surgeon Dr Sirichand, Dr Kamran Khan and Dr Daniyal Mirza of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre, and Dr Mohammed Yaseen, the admin in-charge of the police surgeon office, were the other members of the board. However, in the early hours of Friday, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed to Prof Dr Zakiuddin from DUHS, Prof Dr Kazi Akbar and Prof Dr Abid Hussain Chang from Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences, and Hyderabad Police Surgeon Dr Waseem Khan. On Friday morning, Raza’s family was present at the Tariq Road graveyard for the exhumation, which was then deferred. SC sets aside orders to restore BISP retailer’s blocked ID. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Saturday ruled that a complaint filed by a Point-of-Sale (PoS) agent against the Ben­azir Income Support Programme (BISP) over the blocking of his retailer ID was not maintainable under consumer protection laws, as the relationship did not constitute a “consumer service” arrangement. A two-judge SC bench, headed by Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar, issued the verdict on an appeal filed by BISP Deputy Director Muhammad Ishaq against the Nov 6, 2025 order of the Peshawar High Court, Bannu bench, in a consumer protection appeal. The Supreme Court, however, set aside the judgements of the Consumer Protection Court, Bannu, as well as the PHC, which had earlier directed the BISP and Bank Alfalah to restore the agent’s ID. “We held that [the] complaint under Section 13 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Consumer Protection Act of 1997 was not maintainable,” observed Mazhar in a 14-page order. Rules Point-of-Sale agent cannot invoke consumer law However, in the interest of justice, the Supreme Court also directed the BISP director general (cash transfer), Islamabad, to conduct an inquiry and afford ample opportunity of hearing to respondent Fardayaz Khan, the complainant, to explain the reasons for blocking his alleged PoS agent’s ID. The authority was also directed to confront him with any complaint received against him by the BISP Directorate and then pass an appropriate order within 45 days, so that he may have recourse to an appropriate remedy in accordance with law. The case was initiated by the respondent, who claimed to be a PoS retailer operating under a franchise agreement for distributing BISP payments. His ID was deactivated by Bank Alfalah in May 2021. After his complaint to the Wafaqi Mohtasib was dismissed, he approached the Consumer Protection Court under the KP Consumer Prote­ction Act, nearly two years later. The Consumer Court had on July 1, 2025 issued directives for the BISP and Bank Alfalah to restore Fardayaz Khan’s ID or provide written reasons for its blockage, even though there was no proof of any action taken by the BISP in this regard. Justice Mazhar observed that the complainant was himself a service provider as a retailer and not a “service acquirer” entitled to claim the benefits of the BISP Act, 2010. The judgement noted that no contract or consumer relationship existed between the complainant and the BISP. Since the substratum of the complaint was defective from its inception, the verdict said, the complaint was not maintainable and was liable to be dismissed. The Supreme Court also highlighted that the complainant’s name did not app­ear in BISP’s list of PoS agents for Bannu district, which belied his contention. Justice Mazhar explained that the universal aim of consumer protection laws was to safeguard consumers’ int­e­­rests from unscrupulous and deceptive business practices. In order to counterbalance the imbalance between corporations/manufacturers/service providers and consumers, the right to information, choice and a forum for redressal is also provided to ensure fair treatment on the trading floor, the judgement observed. This special law ensures that products are safe for use and prevents the sale of defective goods, proscribes deceitful advertising, disingenuous pricing and unfair contracts, ensures clear and accurate information about products, and provides procedures for consumers to seek refunds, replacements or repairs and file complaints against fraudulent business activities, the judgement said. The main focus of consumer protection laws globally is to keep sellers honest and protect purchasers of go­­­­ods from fraudulent or deceptive ma­­r­­­­keting or unfair marketing gimmicks. “These laws are vigorous for modern society so that the consumers may be treated fairly and squarely and can seek justice against defective goods and services while maintaining equilibrium in the power dynamics between consumers and conglomerates ethically with the tools to address disputes or complaints,” the verdict said. It added that such protection was necessary because advertisements for products sometimes mislead consumers with exaggerated claims about their products or services but fail to meet the expected quality or result. At other times, they carry hidden fees or confusing clauses that amount to unfair business practices. In recent times, consumer protection laws have also covered e-commerce and digital transactions globally, with the same level of fairness, transparency and consumer rights as brick-and-mortar stores, the judgement said. When diesel prices increased sharply, the PMA’s payment increased slightly, but the company’s actual fuel expense increased much more,” the official, requesting anonymity, explained. “A new formula was devised that reduced this gap but did not eliminate it, forcing the company to pay the remaining fuel costs from its own funds and borrowings, resulting in continuous losses and additional costs.” To a question, he said the court in its orders of June 8, 2023 had directed the PMA to provide from its own sources. IHC seeks govt reply over withholding tax hike on goods transportation. • Petitioners term concessional treatment of oil tanker contractors ‘discriminatory’ • Argue distinction based merely on nature of goods being transported ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has sought responses from the federal government, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and other respondents on a petition challenging the increase in withholding tax (WHT) on goods transportation from 6pc to 7pc through the Finance Act, 2026 . During the hearing, the counsel argued that the enhanced WHT was discriminatory, particularly in view of the concessional tax regime available to oil tanker contractors under the Second Schedule of the Income Tax Ordinance. He contended that the same prime movers and transport infrastructure were being used for carrying petroleum products and other goods of similar capacity. However, an oil tanker carrying petroleum products was subjected to withholding tax at 2pc, while the same vehicle, when used to transport other goods, attracted 7pc WHT. According to the counsel, the distinction was based merely on the nature of goods being transported and had no rational basis. He argued that the differential treatment violated Articles 4 and 25 of the Constitution, which guaranteed protection of law and equality before law. ‘No justification’ The counsel further questioned the basis for increasing the withholding tax from 6pc to 7pc, submitting that no publicly available economic impact assessment or empirical study had been conducted to justify the additional tax burden on goods transporters. He argued that oil tanker operators had historically been given concessional tax treatment because any strike by them could disrupt fuel supplies across the country. On the other hand, goods transport operators, despite providing the same basic transportation service and not resorting to such measures, were subjected to a substantially higher withholding tax. The petitioners maintained that the impugned amendment created an unreasonable and discriminatory classification betwe­­en transport operators performing essentially the same service. After hearing the preliminary arguments, the IHC bench issued notices to the federal government, the FBR and other respondents. As the petition also challenged the constitutional validity of statutory provisions, the court directed issuance of a notice to the AGP. The respondents have been asked to respond to the petition before the matter is taken up on Sept 17. Through the Finance Act, 2026, the federal government revised the withholding tax regime on services, with rates increased from 6pc to 7pc for services such as courier, logistics, hotel, transport, air cargo, car rental, human resource outsourcing and oil drilling. Currently, a large number of local companies, in joint ventures with national and multinational companies, are enga­ged in extracting gold from rivers and streams across GB. According to the GBEPA, it had been observed that heavy machinery was being used for gold extraction from riverbeds and streams, mostly near brid­ges, roads, government and pri­­vate infrastructure, human settlements and agricultural land. Oil and other materials lea­king from generators and other machinery used in the extraction process were also mixing with river and stream water. It had also been observed that untreated wash water generated from gold-washing activities, along with debris, was being discharged into rivers without any sedimentation or settling mechanism. The polluted river water was being used by people in many areas for drinking and other daily needs. The GBEPA said the construction of protection walls along riverbanks for gold extraction and the use of excavated material altered the natural flow of rivers and streams, diverting water towards roads, bridges, human settlements, infrastructure and agricultural land. Such damage could be particularly severe during periods of high river discharge. Furthermore, the dumping of excavated material could cause serious and irreversible damage to sensitive infrastructure. No proper campsites had been established at the project sites, while no appropriate mechanisms had been provided for the safe collection and disposal of solid waste. Adequate sanitation and restroom facilities had also not been provided for workers at the sites, resulting in improper waste management. “These actions constitute a breach of the environmental conditions of approval and endanger public health and safety,” the GBEPA said, adding that they had also caused environmental degradation. The notification ordered that all project operations cease with immediate effect. The project premises had already been sealed by the competent authority. The notification also direc­ted the company to immediate­­ly comply with environmental laws. Mr Hussain said the GBEPA and the minerals department lacked sufficient human resources to monitor mining activities and enforce environmental protection laws at gold extraction sites across GB. Price of collecting BISP stipend. • Agents deducting Rs1,500 to Rs2,000 from payments, say beneficiaries • BISP introduces Social Protection Wallet to reduce dependence on agents WHEN Koonj Jhanjhanjo finally received Rs12,500 from a Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) agent, she had little choice but to accept that Rs11,620 of the amount due to her had been withheld. Along with her husband, Saghir, she spent an entire afternoon in the scorching heat, hoping to receive the remaining amount after the device operator — an agent authorised by BISP and a partner bank to make disbursements — refused to pay what was owed to her. “When we insisted, the operator replied arrogantly that the rest of the amount would be paid later. We objected but finally received the money (despite the massive deduction), after an agonising wait in scorching heat,” her husband told Dawn . Koonj, whose husband is a daily-wage earner, is a BISP beneficiary from the Husri area of Hyderabad. Her entitlement includes financial support under the Benazir Taleemi Wazaif and Benazir Kafaalat programmes, the latter being BISP’s principal social protection arm. Agents authorised by banks and BISP to distribute money through biometric verification usually tell women beneficiaries to take what is being offered or leave it, according to beneficiaries. The deductions are generally lower than in Koonj’s case, usually ranging between Rs1,500 and Rs2,000. Even if her case is an outlier, the scale of smaller deductions is huge. Hyderabad alone has around 44,000 beneficiaries. If Rs2,000 is taken from each beneficiary, agents could potentially pocket an estimated Rs88 million in a single disbursement cycle in just one district. Rehana Keerio from Tando Allahyar and Hasina from Hyderabad faced similar ordeals. Rehana’s son Rafique said he complained to BISP after his mother received Rs17,000 out of an entitlement of Rs19,000. “Agents don’t pay the full amount despite protests by women in every disbursement,” said Hasina’s husband, Ameer Ali, in Hala Naka. The Benazir Kafaalat Programme provides an unconditional quarterly stipend of Rs14,500 to each beneficiary, up from Rs13,500 in the previous two disbursement cycles, according to BISP officials. Yet many women continue to complain of arbitrary deductions while receiving regular tranches under the flagship social welfare programme, which has a budget of more than Rs722 billion. The programme covers 10.2m benefici­aries nationwide, including 2.6m in Sin­­­dh, providing socioeconomic support to some of the country’s most vulnerable households. A married woman is registered after a socioeconomic survey. After receiving her first Kafaalat stipend, she can apply for the conditional Benazir Taleemi Wazaif programme for her children. Meanwhile, the Benazir Nashonuma programme seeks to address stunting and maternal malnutrition. An FIA officer associated with a crackdown on illegal deductions acknowledged that many BISP beneficiaries came from remote areas and found it difficult to pursue complaints or even approach the agency against such malpractices. Unending deductions For quarterly disbursements, BISP partners with six banks to distribute cash through “campsite” and “retail shop” models. Retail shops are operated by private agents, while campsites are temporary BISP facilities established in government buildings, where beneficiaries receive cash in the presence of officials. However, women have complained of unfair deductions at both campsites and retail shops. Under the retail model, partner banks provide agents to BISP through their franchises in different areas. Agents work on a commission-based ar­­rangement and are provided devices by banks exclusively for BISP transactions, a banker said, adding that the device rem­a­ins with them unless they are blacklisted. Agents disburse money from their shops after securing “BISP rights” from a partner bank, which is supposed to provide BISP with lists of agents for physical verification. The lists are shared 48 hours before disbursement, a BISP official said. The verification process is meant to keep blacklisted agents out, but officials allege that it is sometimes compromised, allowing agents with blacklisted records to return to the system. However, the banker disputed the banks’ role in the problem, saying disbursement procedures were finalised by BISP. There is also an Integrated Grievance Management System for registering complaints, but officials said the relatively new system did not contain details of payments made to beneficiaries during the July disbursement. An official said the absence of payment details in the system left BISP officials without an effective means to verify allegations of deductions during that cycle. Cashless model The authorities have now introduced a Social Protection Wallet in an attempt to curb illegal deductions, although the problem has persisted during the transition towards a cashless payment system. Under the programme, SIMs are provided to beneficiaries, who become bank clients with digital accounts. According to a bank official, the system is expected to substantially reduce the role of agents and middlemen and, as a result, the unfair deductions faced by BISP beneficiaries. “Around 30pc of SIMs are activated, whereas 94pc of beneficiaries have so far received SIMs,” Sindh BISP Director General Nasrullah Rind said. “A woman can draw the whole or part of a stipend from any bank. The amount will remain in her account,” he added. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

The team was selected and trained by the Pakis­tan Institute of Engi­neer­ing and Applied Sciences (PIEAS), under the auspi­ces of the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC). Muhammad Ali from Govt College University, Lahore, won a gold medal, while Muhammad Usman from F.G. Sir Syed College, The Mall, Rawalpindi, and Seerat Fatima from Nixor College, Karachi, secured silver medals. Syed Shuja Haider from Sundar STEM School, Lahore, also represented Pakistan at the Olympiad. The students were selec­­ted through the Pakis­tan Nuclear Science Olymp­ia­­­d, an initiative of PAEC ai­­m­ed at identifying and nurturing young scientific talent for participation in the International Nuclear Science Olympiad. In another developme­­nt, Pakistan was annou­n­ced as the host of the 4th In­­ternational Nuclear Sci­ence Olympiad in 2027. On the occasion, Dr Mu­­hammad Maqsood from the PAEC Directorate of Edu­cation and Dr Sajjad Tahir from PIEAS received a commemorative memento. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

Flour prices rising as govt yet to issue import tender. KARACHI: Consumers continued to face rising prices for wheat and wheat flour as the federal government plans to import one million tonnes of grain to curb the escalating costs. According to the Sensitive Price Index data as at Aug 6, the prices of 20 kg wheat flour, 10 kg wheat bag and one kg fine flour have further increased in Karachi to Rs2,700-3,000, Rs1,200 and Rs158.56, up from Rs2,600-2,900, Rs1,160 and Rs149.46, respectively, prevailing at the week ending July 30. The national average prices of a 20 kg flour bag, 10 kg wheat, and 1 kg fine flour for the week ending Aug 6 were Rs2,200-3,133, Rs1,235, and Rs153, as compared to Rs2,200-3,133, Rs1,223, and Rs152.14 for the week ending July 30. In the above period, wheat flour price has risen by 0.52pc. Traders said that the government is not paying any attention to the rising prices of wheat and wheat flour ahead of one million wheat imports. If the government does not bother to control prices before the arrival of imported wheat, consumers will not derive any substantial benefit from this decision. As per SPI data, in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, 10 kg wheat bag prices are the highest at Rs1,339.31, forcing consumers to pay Rs3,040-3,133 for a 20 kg wheat flour bag, followed by Rs173.68 per kg of fine flour, compared to other cities. As provinces are outlining their plans and requirements for wheat, the Sindh Cabinet on Wednesday approved the import of 500,000 tonnes of wheat through the Trading Corporation of Pakistan under the framework being coordinated by the federal government. Punjab plans to import one million tonnes followed by 200,000 tonnes by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 57,500 tonnes by Balochistan. Karachi Wholesalers Grocers Association (KWGA) Chairman Rauf Ibrahim said the government needs to expedite its efforts to curb wheat hoarding by vested interests and speculators who have already plunged into the commodity business. He said the government is taking too long to issue a tender for wheat imports, as it will take a few months for imported wheat to reach Pakistan, while the new wheat crops will arrive in March-May 2027. Fire extinguished at Aramco refinery in Jazan, Saudi Arabia says. Firefighters extinguished a fire that broke out early on Sunday at a facility at Aramco’s Jazan refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi Energy Ministry said, adding that there were no injuries. Aramco’s industrial security teams had brought the fire under control and the relevant authorities were completing procedures to deal with the incident, the ministry said on X. It did not say what caused the fire. The Jazan refinery processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day and produces refined products including gasoline and ultra-light sulfur diesel. Aramco shut down the refinery on July 27 following an attack by Yemen’s Houthi rebels that damaged the plant’s Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) complex and tank farm area, according to a note from consultancy IIR seen by Reuters . The Houthis said at the time they had struck Aramco sites in Jazan and Yanbu. The attacks raised the prospect that threats to Red Sea shipping and Saudi oil infrastructure could widen global disruption stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran and Iranian attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz. Aramco chief Amin Nasser said last week that recent attacks on the company’s facilities had caused some production interruptions but that he was confident operations could be restored quickly. He said the attacks had no material operational or financial impact.

Makkah agreement. IN the midst of a gruelling war between the US and Iran — currently at a stalemate — the signing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday is a highly symbolic development. It comes at a time when the American defence umbrella has proved of little help in protecting Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf Arab states. Rather, the presence of US military assets in these states has pulled them into the war, as the Iranians and their regional armed allies target these facilities. Seen in this context, many questions swirl around the new defence agreement, specifically the fact that it considers an attack against one signatory to be an attack against all. The prime minister, the Saudi crown prince and the Turkish president were all upbeat about the new pact. PM Shehbaz Sharif termed it “historic”, while President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said it is open to “friendly nations”. This is not an ‘Islamic Nato’. Moreover, similar alliances have been attempted before, such as the Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition founded in 2015 and headed by former army chief Gen Raheel Sharif. The latter alliance is not linked to any major operations. Pakistani-Saudi defence collaboration goes back decades, and the current pact only solidifies the arrangement, while also bringing Turkiye on board. But the question in many minds is what role the pact will play vis-à-vis Iran. A Saudi deputy minister has said the agreement “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc”. This clarification is welcome. On the other hand, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader has said that more cooperation among regional states “can secure its security”. If the US-Iran war remains unresolved and major hostilities erupt again, the new alliance will be put to the test, especially if Tehran resumes attacks on the pro-America GCC states. Suffice it to say, such alliances should work to reduce tensions between Muslims states, and not be used against any Muslim country. The US has shown it is uninterested in protecting its Gulf allies, even though the latter have purchased billions of dollars’ worth of weaponry from it. Instead of depending on the US or other foreign powers for security, regional states — indeed all OIC members — should pledge to refrain from aggression against each other. Iran should stop attacking the GCC states, while the Gulf sheikhdoms should stop foreign forces from using their soil against Iran. The Arabs and the Iranians cannot change their geography; they have to live side by side; hence it would be best if they worked out a modus vivendi for mutual security. Hopefully, the new defence agreement can promote unity within the Muslim world, instead of adding to the existing fissures. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

Counterterrorism paradox. PAKISTAN’S security forces are fighting terrorism with commitment and high intensity. From sanitisation campaigns and intelligence-based operations to targeted raids and large-scale engagements, the tempo of action is rising. Yet terrorist violence is not receding. July recorded the year’s highest number of attacks , underscoring the grim reality that the security situation is deteriorating, particularly in KP and Balochistan, despite mounting operational pressure on terrorist groups. The return of violence to areas once declared cleared of terrorism is especially troubling. Last week, Swat suffered a devastating suicide bombing outside the Kabal police station. The attacker struck as participants were leaving the Swat People’s Peace Uprising, organised by residents and civil society groups alarmed by renewed terrorist activity in the valley. Seventeen people, including police personnel and civilians, were killed, while more than a dozen were wounded. Though there is confusion about whether the TTP had targeted the peace rally or the police station, whatever the group’s intentions, the attack raises a significant question about how and why the terrorists are increasing their operational base. Balochistan, meanwhile, experienced one of its worst months of violence in recent years. July saw coordinated, high-impact attacks across Mastung, Lasbela, Ziarat, Kech and Khuzdar. These incidents demonstrated both the geographic reach of armed terrorist groups and their ability to challenge the state simultaneously in dispersed locations. The security response was substantial. According to data maintained by the Pak Institute for Peace Studies, 26 anti-militant operations were recorded across Pakistan in July, compared with 24 in June. Conducted mainly by the army, Frontier Corps and police counterterrorism departments, these operations killed 205 terrorists. Eighteen operations took place in Balochistan and eight in KP. In Quetta and the adjoining Shaban and Hanna Urak areas alone, six operations reportedly killed 68 militants. The country lacks a coordinated strategy that converts operational success into durable peace. These figures reveal both capability and imbalance. Only five suspected terrorists were arrested during the month, all in Karachi. They were allegedly affiliated with the banned Balochistan Liberation Army, Jamaatul Ahrar and Lashkar-i-Jhangvi. The overwhelming ratio of deaths to arrests suggests an increasing reliance on lethal force and a weakness in the investigative, prosecutorial and intelligence-gathering dimensions of counterterrorism. Arrests can expose facilitators, financiers, recruiters and communication networks; dead militants rarely do. Meanwhile, human rights groups continue to express concern over enforced disappearances, deepening mistrust in already alienated communities. In KP, the threat remains centred on the banned TTP and allied factions, including the Hafiz Gul Bahadur group. Since violence resurged in 2021, attacks have been concentrated largely in the southern districts and former tribal areas. Since early 2026, however, the operational map has widened. Militants are increasingly testing settled districts and extending networks towards Balo­chistan and potentially southern Punjab. Their continued mobility and logistical reach, despite sustained operations, show that they retain recruitment, facilitation and support structures. Their tactics are also evolving. Suicide bombings, targeted killings and assaults on police and military installations remain central, but militants are increasingly experimenting with quadcopters and drones for explosive attacks. Government officials, civilians and public infrastructure are also being targeted. The objective is broader than producing casualties: it is to erode state authority, frighten communities and disrupt everyday governance. Public anger over counterterrorism methods adds another layer of risk. The residents of Hassankhel recently protested outside the Peshawar Press Club against alleged drone strikes in their area. They claimed that civilians, including women and children, had been killed and that schools, mosques and roads had been damaged. Whether or not each allegation is established, such protests must be investigated transparently. Civilian harm, or even the perception that it is being ignored, provides militants with propaganda and weakens cooperation between communities and the state. The regional dimension further complicates the challenge. Islamabad’s attempts to pursue Kabul on the TTP sanctuaries inside Afghanistan have not yielded results, and cross-border networks remain a major internal security concern. Still, escalating hostility with Afghanistan cannot substitute for a coherent domestic strategy. Border pressure may constrain the terrorists; it cannot repair governance deficits, police weaknesses or local alienation. Recent counterterrorism operations in Bannu, Quetta and elsewhere confirm considerable operational capacity; however, whether these are translating into long-term success is not clear. The harder question is whether or not tactical successes are producing strategic stability. The evidence suggests they are not. Sanitising an area is not the same as securing it; killing militants is not the same as dismantling the ecosystem that sustains militancy. In a similar context, Balochistan presents an even more complex landscape. Violent Baloch organisations operate alongside religiously inspi­red terrorist groups such as the TTP and IS-K. The province’s vast territory, difficult terrain and thin administrative presence allow militants to disrupt roads, movement and economic activity before security forces can respond. But geography explains only part of the problem. Political exclusion, socioeconomic deprivation, weak public services and a distrust of state institutions create openings that terrorists exploit, particularly among frustrated youth. Saner voices among politicians and intellectuals have long advised that a political solution must be given a full chance and should not be abandoned along the way. Civilian governance must occupy the space rec­overed by security forces. Functional local ad­­min­istrations, reliable services, political engagement and employment opportunities can deny terroris­ts the grievances they weaponise. Commu­ni­ties shou­­ld be treated as partners, not merely as populations to be controlled; their knowledge can strengthen early warning and prevent infiltration. Pakistan’s problem, therefore, is not a shortage of operations. It is the absence of a coordinated strategy that converts operational successes into durable peace. Without accountable governance, political inclusion, capable policing, regional diplomacy and community trust, the state will keep clearing the same ground, and terrorists will keep returning to it. The stakes are now dangerously high nationwide. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

Ban: to what end?. IN April I was living in Islamabad, in a leafy neighbourhood I had moved to after a few months cooped up in the Red Zone. The talks were on and the city was full of foreign correspondents. We passed a coffee shop on our way out of town and half the café was press. What I remember is how much everybody loved Islamabad. On camera and off it. The hills, the food, the hospitality. Testimonials. The state was delighted, and none of it required a form. It is August now. Those same correspondents cannot travel to any city outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi to produce a story without a No Objection Certificate from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The fixers who drove them around must register on a government portal, as must freelancers, translators and camera operators. For a weekend in Murree, a journalist may apply. Permission may be granted within three working days. Feted in April. Registered in August. We do not even change the cast. And Al Jazeera ’s website has not opened from my desk in Karachi since last Sunday. Two browsers, a phone on mobile data. The page sits there and gives up. No order has been published. The PTA has confirmed nothing. What the ministry did say was that it had taken note of Al Jazeera ’s “selective reporting”, that the channel had sought to “misrepresent” the elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and that such “yellow journalism” confirmed the agenda of external actors with vested interests. A government may say that. It should contest any report it dislikes, and it has every means to do so. Restricting access to the report is the thing nobody has put in writing. That distinction matters more than it sounds. A rebuttal adds to the record. A block subtracts from it, and what it subtracts is not the story. It is the ability to check the story. What exactly did the Al Jazeera ban achieve? Because the appetite does not disappear when the reporting does. Nobody stops wanting to know. They simply take what is left, and what is left is whatever costs nothing to produce. Reporting from a difficult district costs money, time, risk and now paperwork. A monologue about that district, filmed in a bedroom in Lahore or London, costs nothing and is regulated by nobody. Every restriction we impose falls on the expensive, checkable kind of journalism and leaves the cheap, unverifiable kind entirely untouched. Then, when a figure appears that the state does not like, it has no way to disprove it. It has spent years dismantling the means by which anything could be disproved. The number stands, uncheckable, and the denial is worth exactly as much as the claim. So, what does a ban achieve? YouTube was blocked in September 2012 for three years. The film that caused it was never removed from the internet. Anyone determined used a proxy. Parliament passed a unanimous resolution asking for it to end. It lifted only because Google agreed to launch a local version. X was blocked in February 2024 after being used to raise allegations of election fraud. It returned 15 months later. VPN use is estimated to have risen 6,000 per cent, and Pakistan recorded the highest financial losses in the world from internet restrictions that year. Cabinet ministers used VPNs to reach the platform their own government had blocked. Al Jazeera was blocked once before, in 2013, after publishing the Abbottabad Commission report. The report was read worldwide. None achieved what the ban was for. Each one ended, but not one because it ‘worked’. What survived each was the impression that the state had something to hide, the one outcome a ban cannot reverse. We are told each time that this is an exception. A parti­cular provocation, a particular mom­ent. The Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines, 2026, remove that alibi. They are not a response to anything. They are the permanent version. On Wednesday, the BBC said it was “extremely concerned” and called for the restrictions to be reversed. Its statement noted that it reaches around 8.6 million people in Pakistan every week, and that its journalists, including local staff here, must be able to travel the country to hear the voices of ordinary citizens. This is what the ban achieved. Not less scrutiny. A BBC statement, a joint appeal from local and international rights groups, and a week of coverage abroad about Pakistan restricting the press. The ministry warned of external actors with vested interests. Then it went and produced them. A confident state does not need to clear the room before it makes its case. It makes the case. So, who will be left to say what happened. And when nobody is, whose account will we be arguing about next? The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi. Infantino denies allegations of affair, favouritism while at UEFA. PARIS: FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now shelved private investment plan, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA. According to The Telegraph , the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football’s governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship. Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article which was published late on Friday. When contacted by AFP on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded. According to The Telegraph , which did not cite its sources, this employee received a “a six-figure sum” upon her departure — at an unspecified time — in addition to the payment of tuition fees for a business school amounting to around 45,000 ($60,700). When contacted by AFP , UEFA acknowledged that “a departure payment was made to the individual in question” at that time, “coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school”. However, it insisted “the payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time”, before adding that “such regulations have been tightened since 2016”. Quoted by The Telegraph , a FIFA spokesperson stated that Infantino, who has been married since 2001, “strongly denies these allegations”, which were “categorically untrue”. “Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” FIFA added. “No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Infantino’s behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved.” Infantino, who is standing for re-election next March, has been embroiled in a crisis since the announcement late last month of his controversial — and ultimately abandoned — plan to open up the World Cup to private investors. He faces opposition in particular from UEFA, which on Thursday stood by its threat to boycott the World Cups, deeming the mere withdrawal of the controversial plan to be insufficient.
