SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE OUTRAGE MACHINE. A short video recently circulating on social media shows Adolf Hitler drinking from a can of Fanta while angrily proclaiming, “I hate juice.” Though millions mistook it for an authentic commercial, sparking fierce online debate, it is actually an AI-generated meme. Its artificial nature is fairly obvious, given that the colour, fonts and logo on the can look nothing like actual Fanta packaging. So why did so many people fall for it? The answer lies in our current media topography, where “shockvertising” has been methodically normalised. The term ‘shockvertising’ emerged in the early 1990s, though the practice dates back to public health campaigns in the late 1960s, and describes a marketing strategy that deliberately violates social, moral or aesthetic boundaries to startle, offend or disturb an audience. Unlike traditional advertisements that highlight product benefits, shockvertising relies on instinctive reactions like fear, disgust, horror or outrage to cut through commercial noise. This is done to drive high brand recall and generate free publicity. Due to the fact that real brands have pushed boundaries in the recent past, a concept as absurd as a Hitler-themed Fanta advertisement suddenly felt plausible to an over-stimulated public. In an online world where algorithms reward anger over accuracy, outrage has become one of the most valuable forms of currency in the digital age The earliest examples of shockvertising emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s through Western government funded anti-smoking campaigns, which featured graphic images of diseased lungs. While these visuals shocked audiences, the public largely accepted them because they served the purpose of raising awareness about smoking-related illnesses. Eventually, governments made it a legal requirement for tobacco companies to print these graphic images directly on cigarette packets. Seeing how receptive people were to shocking imagery when tied to a meaningful cause, and recognising its power to ignite widespread public debate, several consumer brands decided to adopt similar tactics to shatter the clutter of traditional advertising. In the late 1980s, Italian clothing brand United Colours of Benetton transformed shockvertising into a corporate strategy. Instead of displaying clothes, Benetton ran controversial photographs of a dying AIDS activist, a priest kissing a nun and blood-soaked war uniforms, linking the brand directly to concentrated social debates. Luxury brands such as Gucci and Tom Ford later introduced hyper-sexualised, taboo imagery to build an ‘edgy’, exclusive identity, often actively courting media bans to secure free publicity. Illustration by Abro Modern shock tactics have since migrated online, leaning heavily into ‘rage-baiting’ and controversial social stances engineered specifically to drive viral outrage, heated debate and clicks across digital platforms. Shockvertising is an offshoot of what is often referred to as the “outrage economy.” American media theorists Tim Wu and Shoshana Zuboff describe the outrage economy as a digital marketplace where human attention is monetised through heightened conflict and anger. Rather than promoting a brand on its merits or presenting a topic through objective analysis, the outrage economy banks on manufactured outrage to bypass critical thinking, instantly capturing attention and high digital traffic through viral sharing and continuous debate. Social media ‘influencers’ and vloggers frequently resort to making absurd claims and spreading outright falsehoods, purely to inflate their views and comment sections. Far from discouraging this behaviour, social media platforms reward it. Their underlying algorithms are engineered to prioritise high engagement above truth, effectively monetising outrageous content and turning controversy into a business model. Pakistani comedian Tabish Hashmi recently sparked widespread online debate by announcing his departure from a Geo TV show that he hosts. Disappointed fans quickly flooded social media platforms, but their dismay rapidly morphed into outrage after a rumour surfaced claiming Hashmi had been fired over controversial remarks regarding political unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). Remarkably, those expressing outrage rarely paused to verify the nature, or even the existence, of the supposed comments. In reality, no such statements were ever made. The entire episode was a staged publicity stunt. Hashmi was never asked to leave and Geo TV had merely paused production briefly to redesign the show’s set. For days, however, the host and the programme dominated digital discourse. The manufactured controversy allowed observers to project their own political narratives on to the event, with some reading complex state conspiracies into the hiatus and others extending outrage over perceived censorship. The situation raises certain questions about this strategy. Did Geo need to engineer a hoax to boost lagging ratings? But more amusing was the swiftness with which Geo and Hashmi ultimately dismissed the incident as a harmless “prank”. This may suggest a sudden loss of nerve once the audience transformed a routine promotional stunt into a tense conversation about free speech and anti-establishment rhetoric. After the hoax was revealed, many felt disappointed, and even embarrassed, at having been so easily duped. Yet, this vulnerability to manipulation is no longer an anomaly. In an era dominated by swift digital communication and heightened emotional engagement, such impressionability has ceased to be an exception. It has become the standard condition of the modern audience. The media in general and brands are aware of this. It has become easy for manufactured outrage to profit from growing gullibility. When digital platforms actively reward sensationalism over accuracy, critical thinking takes a back seat to knee-jerk reactions. As a result, audiences have grown increasingly susceptible to manufactured narratives, routinely accepting outrage at face value before taking the time to verify basic facts. Politicians, corporate brands, influencers, vloggers, mainstream media outlets and even everyday users all feed this cycle. It is no wonder, then, that the concept of online “trending topics” has so seamlessly replaced genuine public discourse, turning meaningful dialogue into an algorithmic spectacle. To paraphrase the American media theorist Neil Postman, the spectacle is designed for consumption rather than comprehension. Published in Dawn, EOS, August 9th, 2026

Egypt could join Pak-Saudi-Turkiye defence pact once technical issues resolved, says Turkish foreign minister. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday he believed Egypt could join a defence pact signed between Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia once several technical issues were resolved. “Egypt is already our natural partner on all issues. I believe that at the next stage, Egypt will also be among us in the alliance. We already act toward one another as if we were alliance members. There are a few technical issues. Once these are implemented, there is no reason for Egypt not to be part of it,” he told Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu news agency. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed in the Saudi city on Friday, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers the three states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Fidan further elaborated on this, saying the pact was technically the same as Nato’s Article 5 mutual defence agreement. Article 5 of the North Atlantic alliance specifies that an attack on one ​of its members is an attack on all of them. It obliges allies to take action they deem necessary to assist the country under attack, including potentially the use of military force. While the Makkah defence pact stipulates the same, Fidan explained that its text contained general commitments whose practical implementation would depend on discussions and decisions by relevant bodies. A country would need to make a request for assistance and would determine the type of support it needs, he said, adding that the requests could be of different kinds, ranging from intelligence and logistics to ammunition or, if necessary, military units, depending on the scale of the threat. The signatories, he said, would decide through consultations what degree, form, and format of ​support they would ask for in the event of an attack, but that no country would be considered a ​threat as long as a member state is not attacked. Fidan also said that the new alliance was not directed against Iran or any other country, but rather served as a general pledge to support the three signatories’ security. More to follow

Sense of ‘kapwa’ uniquely Filipino – Alex Eala. ENDEAVOR In the aftermath of Alex Eala’s successive victories over the world’s leading tennis players that led to her championship run in Washington, D.C., Rappler released a video clip that her legions of fans should find time to watch. With remarkable humility, she said that her victories are not simply personal wins; but as triumphs that she wants to share with all Filipinos. I watched and listened intently to the reel that was widely shared after landing in Facebook: “Iba talaga ‘pag nakakarinig ng Tagalog, especially sa mga world stages kasi bihira lang nangyayari ‘yun.” (It’s really different when you hear Tagalog being used globally, as that does not happen very often.) She recalls that at age 13, she availed herself of a scholarship offered by the Rafael Nadal Academy situated in Mallorca, off the eastern coast of mainland Span, about 548 kilometers from Madrid and 219 kilometers from Barcelona. There she completed her secondary education from Grade 8 to Grade 11 while undergoing intensive tennis skills development. For her senior year, she transitioned to online private classes through Laurel Springs School, an academic partner of the academy, allowing her to complete her high school diploma while competing full-time on the professional tour. She successfully graduated in 2023. Except for Christmas and New Year interludes when she took the opportunity to return to the Philippines, she studied and lived in Mallorca. Alex narrates that, on account of her round-the-clock immersion and exposure there, she realized that her fluency in her native tongue was diminishing: “Medyo pumapalpak na ang Tagalog ko. So I made it a point na magkaroon ng mga libro na Tagalog. Nakikinig (rin) ako sa OPM (Original Pilipino Music), pinapanood ko yung news…para ma-sustain ko yung level ng Tagalog ko. Indeed, she was always mindful of retaining her Filipino identity through the use of the native tongue: “Malaking bagay ‘yan sa pagiging Pinoy. That’s how people bond. That’s what I don’t see in other people: the sense of kapwa and community. It has brought me blessings. Everywhere I go, ang dami-daming Pinoy na nagpupunta…and not a lot of tennis players get that.” What Alex has underlined as the significance of “pagiging Pinoy”) (or being Filipino) actually affirms the essence and vitality of ‘kapwa’, which is the recognition of our shared humanity and responsibility. By itself, ‘kapwa’ transcends Pinoy uniqueness. It is difficult for non-Filipinos to fully grasp, imbibe or embrace what ‘kapwa’ truly means — and that is the exceptional gift that has propelled Alex Eala to the unparalleled heights of popularity that she has attained. Even her latest opponent, Jessica Pegula, acknowledged that after her championship game versus Alex at Washington, D.C. last week, she received tremendous support from Filipinos who expressed their appreciation to her through social media. Such is the amazing power of ‘kapwa’ or Filipino other-centeredness that Alex Eala’s humility and magnanimity has evoked. As we witness how Alex is lionized by millions across the globe, we begin to realize what has made her a very important celebrity. Alex herself verbalizes this phenomenon. She says that, she feels humbled by the outpouring of love that she experiences from her Filipino admirers on- and off the tennis court. Flashing back to 2022 when she won the US junior championship, Alex said then: “Nagpapasalamat ako sa pamilya ko. Kasi kasi kung hindi dahil sa kanila, hindi ko talaga ito kakayanin. Maraming salamat din sa lahat ng nagdasal at nagsuporta sa akin. Buong puso ko itong ipinaglaban, hindi lang para sa sarili ko kundi para makatulong din ako sa kinabukasan ng Pilipinas. So hindi lang ito panalo ko, panalo nating lahat.” (I wish to thank my family; without their support, I could not have made it here. I also wish to thank all those who supported and prayed for me. I fought with my whole heart to win this, not for myself but to be able to help advance the future and well-being of the Philippines. This is not my triumph alone. This victory belongs to all of us.) Only last Thursday, August 6, she said this after winning her match at the Toronto Open: “Linggo-linggo ko kayong nakikita, sinusuporta ako. Linggo-linggo kong nakikita kung gaano ’nyo kamahal ang kapwa ’nyong Pinoy, kaya proud na proud akong maging Pinoy. Salamat, mga kababayan.” (Every week, I could see and feel your support for me. I could see and feel how much you love me as your fellow Filipino, and that makes me very proud. Thank you, my countrymen.) Seasoned sports observers have noted that while many top-tier players possess the advantages of deep financial privilege or imposing physical frames, Alex Eala plays with the gritty determination of someone carrying the pride of a sports-starved nation. Rather than treating her victories as personal wins, she famously refers to them as shared triumphs for all Filipinos. Hence, fans and sports advocates view her rise not just as an individual milestone, but as a representation of Filipino resilience. It is difficult for non-Filipinos to fully grasp, imbibe or embrace what ‘kapwa’ truly means — and that is the exceptional gift that has propelled Alex Eala to the unparalleled heights of popularity that she has attained. While higher-ranked players enjoy their current ascendancy by dint of their victories on the tennis court, Alex draws massive public support from the millions of Filipinos whose love and admiration for her are rooted in their shared ethnicity — a bond that covers a broad sweep that includes culture and language, ancestry and heritage, traditions and beliefs. A friendship beyond borders: Singapore and the Philippines. By Ambassador Constance See Singapore Ambassador to the Philippines ( Message delivered at the Singapore’s 61st National Day.) Dear readers of Manila Bulletin and friends of Singapore, Singapore celebrates our 61st National Day on Aug. 9. with the theme “Go Beyond.” For a small island nation, going beyond has always meant looking beyond our shores, building trusted relationships and finding common purpose with others. Few relationships illustrate this better than the one Singapore shares with the Philippines. This year marks 57 years of diplomatic relations between our two countries. Over nearly six decades, we have built a multi-faceted and robust partnership spanning trade and investment, innovation, sustainability and, above all, the close connections between our peoples. Serving as Singapore’s Ambassador has given me the extraordinary privilege of meeting. Filipinos from all walks of life across the country. Whether speaking with students, entrepreneurs, public servants, academics or community leaders, I have always been struck by their warmth, creativity, determination and willingness to collaborate to solve problems. Those encounters have made my time in the Philippines deeply rewarding and have further strengthened my confidence in the future of our partnership. People are at the heart of our ties. Today, a large and vibrant Filipino community calls Singapore home. They contribute across healthcare, finance, technology, engineering and many other fields, enriching our society through their skills, dedication and enterprise. Many have also established successful businesses in Singapore. At the same time, a growing number of Singaporeans have built careers and raised families in the Philippines, contributing to the country’s development. They are drawn by the opportunities here, and by the energy and entrepreneurial spirit of the Filipino people. These people-to-people ties are reinforced by deep economic linkages. Singapore has long been one of the Philippines’ largest foreign investors, a testament to our confidence in its long-term potential. Behind these investments are enduring partnerships between Singapore and Philippine companies that have created jobs, developed new capabilities and supported growth across many sectors of the economy. Our longstanding friendship gained fresh impetus recently during President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.’s visit to Singapore in July 2026, where he met with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. The leaders agreed to enhance cooperation in areas including artificial intelligence, education and environmental sustainability. Their discussions underscored a shared resolve to keep our partnership future-ready and responsive to the needs of our peoples. President Marcos also met Singaporean business leaders, whose confidence in the Philippine economy is reflected in their expanding investments in, inter alia, data infrastructure, telecommunications and healthcare. Singapore and the Philippines have stood together since the founding of ASEAN in 1967. As fellow founding members, we share a common interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous Southeast Asia where we work together, uphold international law and keep our region open and connected. Singapore is proud to support the Philippines as ASEAN Chair this year and looks forward to building on that momentum when we assume the Chairmanship in 2027. I am grateful for the close ties our two countries have built over the past 57 years. Our relationship has been strengthened not only by agreements between governments or the investments of our companies, but also by the countless and growing connections between our people. I am confident that by continuing to invest in one another’s success, we will create new opportunities for our peoples and contribute to an even stronger ASEAN. Majulah Singapura. Mabuhay ang Pilipinas.

‘Caskets’ are not political arguments. The five caskets scattered across Metro Manila, carrying anti-China and anti-Communist Party of the Philippines-New People’s Army (CPP-NPA) messages, are a disturbing reminder that in a democracy, even a legitimate message can be discredited by the manner in which it is delivered. The caskets reportedly appeared in Manila, Caloocan, Quezon City and Makati on Aug. 7, in locations chosen for maximum public visibility. A subsequent Quezon City police operation identified the driver of a vehicle allegedly used to unload one casket. Investigators were told that different vehicles were used, with drivers reportedly paid ₱8,000 and helpers ₱1,000 each. Those details make the incident more troubling, not necessarily because of what the messages conveyed, but due to the apparent orchestration behind them. If the objective was to condemn China, the CPP-NPA or communist violence, why resort to caskets? Why make death the centerpiece of political persuasion? Why turn public spaces into stages for a spectacle designed to shock before it persuades? Propaganda may be effective at attracting attention. But attention does not necessarily equate to credibility. The public should therefore resist two equally dangerous reactions. The first is to accept the messaging at face value simply because it is packaged dramatically. The second is to dismiss it immediately without asking who organized it, who financed it and what larger objective may lie behind it. There may be more to this operation than the slogans suggest. Its apparent coordination, multiple vehicles, and reported payments warrant serious scrutiny. Authorities must determine whether this was simply an independently organized propaganda stunt or whether individuals, organizations, or other interests deliberately sought to manipulate public sentiment. The investigation, however, must not become an excuse for political speculation. The government should follow the evidence, preserve CCTV and digital records, trace vehicle rentals and payments, identify the organizers and establish who financed and directed the operation. If laws were violated, those responsible should be prosecuted in accordance with due process. The inquiry should continue until the chain of responsibility is established, not merely until convenient individuals are identified. The government should also communicate transparently. Filipinos deserve to know what investigators have established, what remains unverified and what evidence supports official conclusions. That distinction matters in an era when propaganda can spread faster than facts. The public, meanwhile, has a role here. Do not reward theatrical misinformation with instant outrage or unquestioning applause. Verify before sharing. Ask who benefits from the spectacle. Report suspicious activities to authorities. Demand evidence from the government—and accountability from those who manufacture political messaging. There are countless decent ways to oppose communism, criticize China’s policies or denounce violence. Write. Debate. Hold forums. Publish evidence. Organize peaceful assemblies. Present victims’ stories with dignity. Challenge ideas with better ideas. A democratic and just society should have no shortage of courage. What it should have less tolerance for is political theater that treats death as a prop. If the message is worth hearing, it deserves something better than a casket.

My reduction and rejuvenation challenge. HEARD IT THROUGH THE GRIPE-VINE At my age, you get help from wherever you can get it. When the health crisis started in 2020, I was 65 years of age, and considered myself trim and relatively flab-free. A bout with Prostate Cancer in 2021, hormonal shifts, cellular changes, muscle loss, and a decline in my metabolism, have all contributed to what I now hate seeing in the mirror every morning - excess fat in my tummy and flanks. Throughout any given week, I try and maintain an exercise and fitness regimen that alternates tennis, swimming, and some hours in the gym. But my body is slow in responding - and that’s why I mention ‘help’. My friends readily admit to using Ozempic or Mounjaro, which belong to a class of medications known as GLP-1 receptor agonists. These mimic a gut hormone to curb appetite, while stabilizing one’s blood sugar. They’re extremely happy with the results, but as they involve weekly subcutaneous injections, I’ve not joined that particular bandwagon - and don’t intend to. What I have begun on a regular basis since the second quarter of 2026, are twice-weekly sessions at Marie France - non-invasive RF protocols that I’m counting on to help reduce the excess fat via contouring and lymphatic drainage. At the start of the week, I have an Endospheres session; then towards the end of the week, I have a TMP (Thermo Magnetic Pulse) session. They both take less than an hour, and now that I’m on my 4th month, I’ve discerned the changes and improvement. Periodically, I also drop by Facial Care - right across Marie France at their BGC location, for the Optimas Forma treatment. These sessions are supplementary to my exercise regimen, and I do try and be careful about my food intake - so I’m not dependent on these sessions alone. The EndoSpheres machine is FDA-approved, and utilizes compressive microvibration technology. A handheld cylinder that’s equipped with some 50-55 rotating silicone spheres activate low frequency mechanical vibrations that according to the literature boost lymphatic drainage, increase blood flow, break down fat cells, and tone your muscle. It results in fat and cellulite reduction, stimulates collagen and elastin production, and can do skin-contouring. The cylinder can ‘attack’ one’s abdomen, the thighs, arms, waist, and flanks. There’s a comfortable warmth to the procedure and its just a matter of getting used to the rotating spheres as they are applied to particular parts of one’s body. The Thermo Magnetic Pulse is regularly done to my tummy and flanks specifically. It’s a non-surgical four-in-one body contouring treatment. The technology is RF (Radio Frequency) driven, coupled with a vacuum suction device. Pulsed electromagnetic fields use heat to break down fat cells, while stimulating collagen production. The promise is to reduce stubborn fat, tighten lax skin, smoothen cellulite, and achieve targeted body contouring. There is heat in this protocol as it is supposed to reach deeper layers of fat tissue. The suction like sensation takes getting used to, and the heat aspect is regulated via the use of a cooling gel that handles temperature sensitivity. This one does require more attention on the part of the technician, as the heat can get uncomfortable after a while, or if the gel has already been absorbed. Over at Facial Care, their Optimas Forma is a medical aesthetic workstation for non-surgical facial rejuvenation. It’s a non-invasive RF treatment that promotes safe skin tightening and contouring - it’s been popularly nicknamed the Red Carpet Facelift. Operating on the same principle of RF, the session involves heating deep layers of facial skin to stimulate new collagen production, and lead to the lifting and tightening of the cheeks, jawline, neck, and the skin area around our eye sockets. It evens skin tone, and reduces redness and blotching. There is a specific applicator used for the eye area so that the heat is applied over a smaller area of skin. I experienced sensitivity on my forehead and temple, and that was attributed to the fact that there’s less skin, and we’re closer to bone. It’s that twinge of heat discomfort at particular spots that were the only things one has to look out for. Relatively painless, and effective over time with frequency, there’s much to recommend with my sessions at both Marie France and Facial Care. They’ve become part of my weekly routine now, and I welcome how they augment what I do in order to maintain my weight, and restore my past form. I still have some way to go to achieve my target and goals; but am happy that it’s being done in a non-invasive manner. It’s about regular visits, and maintaining other habits and patterns to promote health and wellness. Marie France has an ongoing Go Lose Pounds promotion, emphasizing doctor consultations to customize a safe and healthy way to get rid of that excess poundage. It isn’t about short cuts, but about deveoping a proper protocol and program that fits your target and body type.

DOE should deep-six 'build-anywhere' practice of power plants; De Jesus explains why. PHILRECA Party-list Rep. Presley de Jesus has placed the onus on the Department of Energy (DOE) to end its habit of allowing generation companies to build power plants wherever they choose. This, as De Jesus cited in a recent House Committee on Energy hearing that strategic siting near existing transmission facilities was key to reducing technical system losses. De Jesus, a deputy minority leader, questioned whether or not the DOE has a policy requiring generation companies to coordinate with grid operator National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) when selecting project sites. "Napapansin ko dito, kung saan gusto ng generation companies, doon sila nagtatayo. Para ma-minimize ang technical loss, may policy ba kayo? At coordinated ba ito sa NGCP?" he asked. (I notice here that wherever the generation companies want, that’s where they build. To minimize technical loss, do you have a policy? And is this coordinated with NGCP?) The panel hearing, held last Wednesday, Aug. 5, kicked off discussions on the proposed abolition of the system loss charge --seen as an unfair, passed-on charge to consumers. No less that President Marcos called on solons to scrap it during his July 27 State of the Nation Address (SONA). The DOE said it is already coordinating with NGCP through the Transmission Development Plan (TDP) and will require future bidders under the Green Energy Auction (GEA) to consider transmission readiness and proximity to major load centers when choosing plant locations. According to the DOE, the policy aims to reduce technical system losses by shortening the distance electricity travels through the transmission network. The guidelines are expected to be included in the terms of Rrference for the next GEA within the next two months. De Jesus--a member of the "Power Bloc" in the House of Representatives-- urged DOE to move beyond planning and immediately institutionalize the policy. He emphasized that closer coordination with NGCP in siting future power plants was a long-term solution to reducing technical system losses, improving transmission efficiency, and ultimately lowering avoidable costs in the power system.

First Lady hails 200 Filipino children given new lease on life through India liver transplants. First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos has hailed the successful liver transplants performed on 200 Filipino children at an Indian hospital, saying the procedures gave them "a renewed chance to dream, grow and enjoy the childhood they deserve." Araneta-Marcos served as chief guest at a gathering in Makati on Friday, Aug. 7, marking Indraprastha Apollo Hospital's milestone of 200 successful pediatric liver transplants involving children from the Philippines. In a Facebook post after the event, the First Lady described the milestone as "deeply heartwarming" and expressed gratitude to Prof. Anupam Sibal and the Apollo medical team for their work in treating Filipino children with complex liver diseases. "Through your skill, compassion and unwavering dedication, you have not only saved lives -- you have given hope to hundreds of Filipino families," Araneta-Marcos said. She said the milestone showed "just how precious the gift of life truly is," while recognizing the 200 children who were given another opportunity to live, grow, and enjoy their childhood. 200 children, one medical milestone Apollo said the completion of 200 successful pediatric liver transplants for Filipino children marked an important milestone in its pediatric liver transplant program and its long-standing association with Filipino patients and families. Filipino children, it said, have traveled to its New Delhi facility for treatment of conditions including biliary atresia, metabolic liver diseases, and liver cancer, where liver transplantation may be the life-saving option for children with end-stage liver disease. Apollo reported a 93 percent success rate in pediatric liver transplants, although its news release did not specify the period covered by the figure or the measure used to determine "success." Dr. Prathap Reddy, founder chairman of Apollo Hospitals Group, said the milestone reflected the trust Filipino families had placed in the hospital and the advances in clinical expertise and multidisciplinary care for complex pediatric cases. Dr. Anupam Sibal, group medical director and senior pediatric gastroenterologist and hepatologist of Apollo Hospitals Group, said pediatric liver transplantation was among the most complex surgeries, particularly for very small children. Sibal added that Apollo's experience included combined liver-kidney transplants, liver transplants in babies weighing as little as 3.5 kilograms, and ABO-incompatible transplants in which donors and recipients have different blood groups. "Every successful transplant represents a child given a second chance at a healthy life," Sibal said. Dr. Neerav Goyal, senior consultant and head of liver transplant surgery at Indraprastha Apollo Hospital, said treating very small children requires precise surgical planning, meticulous vascular reconstruction and coordination among several medical specialties. Goyal said improvements in surgical techniques, anesthesia, intensive care, and immunosuppression had contributed to improved outcomes, while transplant care continued from evaluation through lifelong follow-up. Recently, Filipino twin toddlers Tyler and Kelly Clarito underwent separate living donor liver transplants at Apollo Hospitals in New Delhi after developing liver failure linked to Choledochal Cyst Type IVA, a rare congenital disorder. Tyler underwent his transplant on May 29, while Kelly followed on June 3, with their mother, Daisy Ann Clarito, donating part of her liver to Tyler and their maternal uncle, Roy Escasinas, donating part of his liver to Kelly. Their father, Wilson Clarito, said the family spent months seeking treatment before the twins were brought to India, where the surgeries and subsequent recovery gave the children a chance to return home. The twins' case also underscored the sacrifices involved in securing a transplant abroad, with their family relying on assistance from several Philippine officials and private supporters for hospital expenses, airfare, and accommodation. Apollo Managing Director Shivakumar Pattabhiraman said the hospital had built long-standing relationships with Filipino patients, families and clinicians who shared the goal of securing timely access to specialized care. The hospital said its Liver Transplant Program has performed more than 5,000 transplants involving patients from 50 countries, while its broader solid organ transplant program has performed more than 28,000 liver, kidney, heart, lung, intestinal, pancreas, and multi-organ transplants. The Manila gathering was attended by Indian Ambassador Harsh Kumar Jain, Sen. Erwin Tulfo, Sen. Bong Go, Sen. Robinhood Padilla, Manila Mayor Francisco "Isko Moreno” Domagoso, Makati Mayor Nancy Binay, and Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) Administrator Patricia Yvonne "PY" Caunan.

ASEAN pushes regular access to Aung San Suu Kyi, reiterates call for unconditional release. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has renewed its call for regular and sustained access to detained Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi and reiterated its demand for her complete and unconditional release following her meeting with an International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) representative. In a recent Chairman’s Statement, the ASEAN, currently chaired by President Marcos, welcomed the Aug. 3 meeting between Suu Kyi and ICRC Resident Representative to Myanmar Arnaud de Baecque, describing it as a positive step toward inclusive national dialogue and reconciliation among all parties in Myanmar. “We view this as a positive step towards inclusive national dialogue and reconciliation among all parties in Myanmar and hope that this will pave the way for regular and sustained access for her family, legal counsel, medical professionals, and appropriate humanitarian representatives,” Marcos said. The bloc also urged the further expansion of access to people detained in Myanmar since February 2021 and reiterated its call for their release, including Suu Kyi's complete and unconditional release. “We believe that further positive steps would contribute to building trust and creating a more conducive environment for lasting peace and stability in Myanmar,” President Marcos said. Five-Point Consensus remains framework The ASEAN chair reaffirmed the continued relevance of the ASEAN Special Envoy on Myanmar in engaging all parties toward an inclusive national dialogue in line with the Five-Point Consensus, which remains the bloc's primary framework for addressing the crisis. “We reiterate the continued relevance of the role of the Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair on Myanmar in engaging all parties concerned towards an inclusive national dialogue, in line with the Five-Point Consensus (5PC),” the statement read. The statement also called for the Special Envoy, currently Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, to be granted access to Myanmar to meet all parties concerned, including Suu Kyi, as part of the envoy's mandate under the Five-Point Consensus. “In this regard, we look forward to the Special Envoy being granted access to visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned, including Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, as part of the Special Envoy’s mandate under the 5PC,” Marcos said. Philippines pushes compliance In her press briefing during the conclusion of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on July 24, Lazaro said ASEAN continued to use the Five-Point Consensus in assessing Myanmar's compliance and participation in ASEAN meetings. She added that ASEAN was developing measurable benchmarks to assess Myanmar's implementation of the consensus and stressed that the issue was not about how many ASEAN members supported or opposed Myanmar's return to high-level meetings. “There's no number, because the issue here is, have they complied with the five-point consensus? If there is compliance, then that means it will change,” Lazaro said. She also said that failure to meet the benchmarks would mean failure to comply with the Five-Point Consensus. “Again, we repeat, we always go back to the five-point consensus,” Lazaro said. The ASEAN chair said the bloc remained committed to helping Myanmar, as an integral part of ASEAN, achieve a peaceful and durable solution to the crisis that is Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led.

31 families evacuated in Muntinlupa. A total of 31 families, or 132 individuals, were evacuated in Muntinlupa as heavy rains continued due to the southwest monsoon. Based on data from the Muntinlupa City government’s Social Services Department, as of 8 a.m. on Aug. 9, 18 families are staying at Bagong Silang Elementary School, 11 families at the DRT covered court in Barangay Putatan, and two families at Villa Carolina Pavilion in Barangay Tunasan. Mayor Ruffy Biazon said the city government continues to monitor situations in different barangays, especially the low-lying areas. The city government activated emergency response measures to respond to any situation. Search and rescue teams, and equipment are on standby. It advised people to conduct a preemptive evacuation if their area is at risk and go to the nearest evacuation area. Parts of barangays in Muntinlupa are situated along the Laguna Lake. As of 7 a.m. on Aug. 9, the Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA) said the average water level at Laguna Lake stood at 11.68 meters or within the normal and safe transition range. The critical high level is 12.5 meters.

Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not open until the US corrects its behavior. Iran's politburo-like body known as the Supreme National Security Council said the Strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States "corrects its behavior," issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway and traffic on it. Iran's state broadcaster published the statement by the council's secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the powerful Revolutionary Guard. The United States must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The U.S. must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must "completely compensate" Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and "unconditionally" release frozen assets. There was no immediate comment from the U.S., which has wanted an acceptable deal first on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and plan on compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets. A 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended. Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi earlier Saturday said they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation, "specifically the determination of a transit route." But the waterway's reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the U.S. violation of the interim deal. Oman, a mediator Gulf Arab country which has said relatively little on the talks, said in a statement Saturday that the discussions were ongoing "in a positive and constructive atmosphere," and condemned attacks on ships on the strait. The strait, crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low. Iran attacks a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, the UAE says A vessel owned by Abu Dhabi's state-owned ADNOC oil and gas company was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier Saturday. The Foreign Ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping. ADNOC in a statement said there were no casualties following the attack early Saturday. The company said over a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while transiting the strait since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said. ADNOC didn't elaborate on the attack's location or any damage. Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman, had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, with the vessel and crew safe. It was not clear whether this was the ADNOC incident. A defense deal is not aimed at any third country, Turkey says A defense agreement that Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed on Friday is not aimed against any third country, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said. It says an attack on one would be considered an attack on all three. Fidan told Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency on Saturday that the countries do not view any state as an adversary unless it takes hostile action against them: "We don't have anything written down — nothing we've signed — that defines a common threat." Asked how the mutual defense mechanism would work, Fidan said a member would formally request help and the two countries' assistance could range from intelligence-sharing to logistics support or the deployment of military units. The mechanism would establish a secretariat to be based in Saudi Arabia, Fidan said. He said other nations, which he did not name, have expressed interest in joining the agreement, adding that he expects Egypt, which he described as a "natural partner," to participate "at the next stage." Yemen's military attacks Iran-backed Houthis The attacks were in response to the Houthis' recent strikes in central and eastern Yemen. Col. Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for Yemen's military, said the attacks targeted the rebels' "sites and capabilities" on multiple front lines, without elaborating. The escalation between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government and its backer, a Saudi-supported coalition, threatens to reignite Yemen's civil war following a 2022 truce. Turkey's Kurdish peace bill wins approval in parliament A Turkish draft law aimed at advancing a peace effort with the country's Kurdish insurgents passed its first hurdle in parliament on Saturday. A committee approved the measure. It is expected to be approved in the general assembly next week. Last year, the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, declared its decision to disarm and disband as part of the peace initiative aimed at ending the decades-long conflict with the Turkish state. The draft legislation defines the procedures for the group's disarmament and rehabilitation of some PKK members. The measures would come into effect once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the group has disbanded and surrendered all weapons. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people since it began in the 1980s. Turkey and its Western allies consider the group a terrorist organization.

CSC suspends August 9 civil service exams in Metro Manila, parts of Luzon amid inclement weather. The Civil Service Commission (CSC) has suspended the Career Service Examination-Pen and Paper Test for the Professional and Subprofessional levels scheduled for Sunday, Aug. 9, in several areas in Luzon due to heavy rains caused by the enhanced southwest monsoon (habagat). The suspension covers all testing centers in the National Capital Region, as well as centers in Batangas, Cavite, Laguna, and Rizal in Region 4, and Baguio, La Trinidad, and Abra in the Cordillera Administrative Region. CSC said the decision was made due to the potential impact of the weather on the safety and accessibility of examinees, examination personnel, and other stakeholders. Affected examinees are advised to monitor the official Facebook pages of the concerned CSC Regional Offices and the commission's official communication channels for updates on the rescheduled examinations and other related announcements.

Turkey says defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is not aimed at Iran or any other country. ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — A defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey is not aimed against Iran or any other country, Turkey's foreign minister said Saturday, describing the pact as an important step toward regional stability. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the agreement in the Saudi holy city of Mecca on Friday. It states that an attack on one would be considered an attack on all three. The "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" brings together oil-rich Saudi Arabia and nuclear power Pakistan as well as Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a rapidly growing defense industry. It deepens cooperation and deterrence at a time of increased regional uncertainty and threats from the war in Iran. In an interview with Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency, Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan insisted that the three countries do not view any particular state as an adversary unless they take hostile action against them. "We don't have anything written down — nothing we've signed — that defines a common threat," Fidan said. "Any country that does not attack us is not a target for us." The Turkish minister described the agreement's clause on mutual defense as being "technically the same" as NATO's Article 5, under which an attack on one of the 32 members is considered an attack on them all. Asked how the mechanism would work, Fidan said a member would need to formally request help and that the other two countries' assistance could range from intelligence sharing to logistic support — or the deployment of military units depending on the threat. "These are multi‑layered matters that vary according to the scale of the threat," Fidan said. "This is the perspective we have set out so far in our work." The Turkish minister said other nations — which he did not name — have expressed interest in joining the agreement, adding that he expects Egypt, which he described as a "natural partner," to participate "at the next stage." Under the deal, the foreign and defense ministers of the three countries, along with their military chiefs, would hold regular committee meetings. The three countries would also establish a secretariat, to be based in Saudi Arabia, Fidan said.

A 12-year-old girl dies after Thailand school shooting, bringing the death toll to at least 8. BANGKOK (AP) — A schoolgirl died from critical wounds on Saturday after a student opened fire at a high school and his home outside Bangkok the day before, bringing the death toll from the attack to at least eight people. The 14-year-old opened fire at around 10 a.m. Friday at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi province northwest of the Thai capital before apparently taking his own life. He also appeared to have killed his two grandparents at his family home earlier in the morning, officials said. The girl, 12, died after hospitalization, the Health Ministry said. The school had posted a message on Facebook Friday seeking blood donations for two students, including the girl, who was in seventh grade. Fourteen people remain hospitalized, of whom seven remain in critical condition Saturday, according to Thailand's Health Ministry. Most of those wounded were between 12 and 14 years old. Relatives claimed the bodies of eight people from Bangkok's Institute of Forensic Medicine: five school staff, the accused shooter, and his grandparents. Emergency workers brought out a coffin and loaded it onto an ambulance, which will transport the bodies to their hometowns for funeral rites. The young girl's body is still to be released. Wiroon Supasingsiripreecha, head of the institute, said most of the victims suffered a single fatal gunshot wound to a vital area, including the chest or head. He said the gunshot wound found on the alleged shooter was consistent with the weapon he had used. More detailed forensic findings, including toxicology results, are expected later, he said. Officials said the gun, described as small and compact, was legally registered to the boy's grandfather. There were reports that the boy, who lived with his grandparents, had shown signs of stress connected to school, although some of his relatives told Thai media that they were unaware of any troubles he might have been facing. The co-educational state school, which has about 3,000 students enrolled aged 12 to 18, said all classes would be suspended between Aug. 10-14 and school staff were instructed to work from home during that time. A few mourners laid flowers Saturday morning at the school's gate, where a few police officers could be seen. Charin Siriananchai brought his two sons, ages 9 and 6, to pay their respects. He said while his sons do not study here, he lives in the neighborhood and drives past this school almost every day, often stopping to allow students to cross the road. "Everyone was saddened and shocked, because it was unexpected that this would happen in Thailand, and also it's quite a great loss," he said. Some parents also came with their children to collect their belongings left behind after the shooting. A father, who declined to identify himself, said his son, who was at the school during the shooting, was still in shock and could not sleep alone. Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia, second only to Pakistan and far surpassing its Southeast Asian neighbors. Data collected in 2017 by the groups Small Arms Survey and GunPolicy.org in their last extensive international study found civilian gun ownership in Thailand was about 15.1 guns per 100 people, compared with less than one per 100 in neighboring Malaysia. Thailand had 3.49 deaths by firearms per 100,000 people, according to 2023 statistics published by World Population Review. That puts it well behind parts of Latin America and the Caribbean, but relatively high in Asia. Only the Philippines is higher in Southeast Asia. While shootings involving indiscriminate killings are not common, the country has seen an uptick in high-profile shooting deaths in recent years. In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand, briefly taking people hostage in a two-hour attack that killed one person and wounded two others. A 14-year-old boy was accused of a 2023 shooting at a major Bangkok shopping mall.

‘Tagay Para Sa Ex’ promises blissful chaos. If you’ve ever been in a friend circle that has a couple that broke up, you know just how messy things can get. Sides are taken, bridges are burned, and the entire group is left hanging in a state of awkward limbo. It’s a frenzy that no one can recover from. “Tagay Para Sa Ex (Cheers for the Ex)” makes for a blissful reminder of the chaos such a scenario brings. “Tagay Para Sa Ex” follows a birthday drinking session of five friends: BPO worker Mark (AJ Sison), his ex-girlfriend Liz (Yesh Burce), a couple in a rocky relationship, Benj (Jel Tarun) and Mich ( Brigitta Marilla), and the one friend who seemingly glues them all together, Poch (Buknoy Gonzales). It’s set within Mark’s condominium, where conversations about love, sex, career, and relationships unfold as a looming storm goes on in the background. Under the direction of Dudz Teraña, we watch as a different kind of storm unfolds within Mark’s condo. As more drinks are shared, loose lips share tales that probably should have stayed private. A Pandora’s box of stored memories comes unfurling through the night as the ex-lovers and current lovers start to spew out their opinions on relationships. These rants and conversations play out almost similarly to how they would in real life, with dialogue often overlapping as some friends start to go off to have their own little conversations. Audience members might feel like flies on the wall watching the slow chaos stirring about and unleashing itself at the peak of the storm. Sometimes, familiar tunes also play during key moments. However, on a personal note, these feel unnecessary to convey the weight of the scene and can even be distracting. The performances are engaging enough to draw you into the atmosphere without relying on familiar music. Every cast member brings a heavy weight to their characters. AJ and Jel can have you either agreeing or outright wanting to throw your seats at them when their characters let out their rather calculated views on love. We feel for the Disney Princess-esque hopes and dreams of the romantic Mich from Briggita. Yesh, as Liz, makes us feel the painful history that her character shares with Mark as she recounts the slow death of their once beautiful spark. Buknoy steals the spotlight every time as Poch, using quick zings delivered in a way that helps cool down such intense moments. Ultimately, it’s a night that is guaranteed to leave you feeling like an emotional rollercoaster. Expect joy, laughter, sorrow, and anger to come in waves.

Monsoon rains wipe out PBA Sunday doubleheader. The heavy downpour and widespread flooding across Metro Manila have forced the PBA to postpone its Season 50 Governors’ Cup doubleheader at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium on Sunday, Aug. 9. The league announced the suspension early Sunday, citing the inclement weather brought by the southwest monsoon intensified by the Typhoon Dolphin which was outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR). “In light of the severe weather conditions, and with the safety of our fans, players, officials, and staff as our top priority, the PBA has decided to postpone its Sunday, August 9 games,” the league said in a statement. The scheduled doubleheader featured the Phoenix Super LPG Fuel Masters against the Rain or Shine Elasto Painters and Barangay Ginebra San Miguel against the Blackwater Bossing at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium. The PBA said the games will be rescheduled, with the updated dates and times to be announced through its official channels. The postponement came as heavy rains battered Metro Manila and other parts of Luzon, causing flooding in several areas and making travel conditions difficult. Last week, several players, coaches and fans were stranded by the heavy rains that caused shin-deep floods around the Malate venue. The games in the last two days at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium and Ynares Center Montalban were also interrupted by several roof leaks brought by the heavy downpour.

‘Dungeons & Dragons’ is having a crossover with ‘Star Wars’. “Dungeons & Dragons (D&D)” is putting out tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) set in the universes of “Star Wars” and “World of Warcraft (WoW).” Wizards of the Coast made the announcement during Gen Con 2026, one of the largest TTRPG gatherings in the US. It’s D&D taking a page from “Magic: The Gathering,” the highly popular trading card game also under Wizards of the Coast that has its own Universes Beyond catalog that crosses over with other genres and franchises like “Doctor Who,” “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles,” and “The Lord of the Rings.” Not much has been revealed about the “Star Wars” crossover other than the campaign season’s title, “Season of Rebellion.” Details also indicate that the timeline is set to take place during the events of the Galactic Civil War, which largely takes place during the Original Trilogy and trickles down to the timeline of “The Mandalorian.” It also hasn’t been revealed if any of the iconic characters are set to be featured heavily in the upcoming crossover, though Darth Vader did make a special appearance during the announcement. From the timeline shown, much of the content is set for release in 2027. As for the WoW crossover, the joint venture with Blizzard Entertainment starts rolling things out with the first book releasing in November. It isn’t leaving any stone unturned, making every species and class from the WoW franchise present in the upcoming collab. Included in the expansion book are details of all the playable characters and classes, over 26 magic items, seven dungeons based in WoW, 30 dungeon boss stat blocks, 50+ new monsters, and 60+ new spells. Pre-orders have already begun, with early access rolling out on Nov. 3. “We want to let our community know that D&D Universes Beyond is additive to the incredible roadmap we have for our own worlds,” shares Wizards of the Coast through a blog post. “We have been staffing up to support this initiative and look forward to what the future holds.”

Intense rains to persist as tropical cyclones enhance ‘habagat’ — PAGASA. Intense rains will continue to batter parts of Luzon and the Visayas through Tuesday, Aug. 11, as two tropical cyclones outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) enhance the southwest monsoon or “habagat,” the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Sunday, Aug. 9. PAGASA weather specialist Aldczar Aurelio said rainy weather is expected to continue over Luzon, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, and Central Visayas due to the habagat. The rest of the Visayas and the entire Mindanao will generally have fair weather, although partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms may still occur. For Sunday, more than 200 millimeters of rainfall, classified as intense to torrential, is expected in Ilocos Sur and Benguet. Rainfall of 100 to 200 millimeters, or heavy to intense, is forecast over La Union, Abra, Zambales, Bataan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro. Meanwhile, 50 to 100 millimeters of moderate to heavy rain is expected in Ilocos Norte, Pangasinan, Apayao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Ifugao, Nueva Vizcaya, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Bulacan, Laguna, Oriental Mindoro, and Antique. The rains are expected to continue into Monday, Aug. 10. Rainfall of 100 to 200 millimeters is forecast over Ilocos Sur, La Union, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan, and Occidental Mindoro, while 50 to 100 millimeters is expected over Ilocos Norte, Pangasinan, Abra, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Ifugao, Nueva Vizcaya, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, Oriental Mindoro, and Antique. On Tuesday, Aug. 11, Zambales, Bataan, and Occidental Mindoro may receive 100 to 200 millimeters of rain. La Union, Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Tarlac, Pampanga, Nueva Ecija, Cavite, Batangas, and Antique may receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall. Aurelio advised the public to remain alert for possible flash floods and landslides, especially in areas that have experienced continuous rainfall over the past few days, as the already saturated soil increases the risk of flooding and landslides. Meanwhile, PAGASA is monitoring three tropical cyclones outside the PAR. Typhoon Dolphin was located 745 kilometers north-northeast of Itbayat, Batanes. “Malabo na itong pumasok sa ating Philippine Area of Responsibility dahil ito'y kikilos pa-kanluran o papunta sa southern part ng China (It is unlikely to enter our Philippine Area of Responsibility because it will move westward toward the southern part of China),” Aurelio said. A tropical depression east of extreme Northern Luzon was located more than 1,980 kilometers east of the area, with maximum sustained winds of 45 kilometers per hour. Aurelio said it is also unlikely to enter the PAR. “Base sa ating mga data at analysis, mababa ang tsansa na pumasok sa ating area of responsibility dahil ito'y kikilos pa-silangan o palayo sa ating bansa (Based on our data and analysis, there is a low chance that it will enter our area of responsibility because it will move eastward, away from the country),” he said. The third tropical depression was located 3,435 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon, also with maximum sustained winds of 45 kilometers per hour. Aurelio said this has a low chance of entering the PAR as it is expected to move away from the Philippines.

Growing up with the arts in postwar Manila. The latest issue of “Backstage Pass,” the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ excellent newsletter, lists events for August: the 22nd season of Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival, three plays from VLF ZZI at Teatro Ignacio Gimenez, the best of ASEAN Performing Arts 2026, Music at Sunset in Intramuros, Kabataang Gitarista 14th Anniversary Recital, and more coming up. Manila’s and the country’s cultural calendar has not been as rich, and I sometimes wonder how I became chairman of the CCP when, like many Filipinos of my generation, I simply absorbed what happened to come my way. I grew up in the 1940s and 1950s, attended Manila public schools, and took up accounting at the University of the Philippines. Looking back, it is clear that my education in the arts was entirely incidental and accidental, formed by chance encounters, curiosity, and unexpected opportunities. My parents were schoolteachers, and we had shelves upon shelves of reading material. With no TV, electronics, or children my age nearby, I spent my time browsing books on history and literature, back issues of the Reader's Digest, an encyclopedia, assorted travel guidebooks, and, of all things, a book on the plots of famous operas. I also devoted much of my allowance to comic books, especially “Classics Illustrated,” which introduced me to works such as “A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court,” “Around the World in Eighty Days,” and “The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.” Even a Sunday magazine became an unlikely classroom, with its playing-card-sized illustrations of famous buildings, historical figures, plants, and curious objects, each accompanied by detailed captions. School added its own unexpected lessons. In Grade Four, our teacher introduced us to gladiators and showed us a reproduction of Juan Luna's “Spoliarium.” She told us the painting was worth what to me was the astronomical (and, of course, hilariously wrong) ₱30,000. We learned the intricacies of flats and sharps in music class; English classes opened doors to literature through poems like Walt Whitman's “O Captain! My Captain!” and Edgar Allan Poe's “Annabel Lee,” the epic “Beowulf,” and Abraham Lincoln's “Gettysburg Address.” One year, our entire third-year class trooped to the Philippine Normal School to watch a production of “The Merchant of Venice,” performed by future teachers as part of their training. School life itself often became a stage. We spent weeks rehearsing “La Jota Moncadeña” before performing it at Rizal Memorial Stadium during what must have been a citywide folk dance festival. My PE teacher picked skinny me to be one of the “maglalatik” dancers, doing our piece outdoors one chilly evening, shirtless but for half a dozen coconut shells. The auditorium, created by folding back movable classroom partitions, regularly hosted programs featuring the whole range of student talent. I once represented my class in a declamation contest on the Bill of Rights. On another occasion, I was complimented for singing the loudest in a choral performance. Cultural opportunities expanded when I went to UP. The Dramatic Guild staged plays by Wilfrido Ma. Guerrero as well as foreign classics, including “A Streetcar Named Desire.” Violetta’s aria “Libiamo” in Verdi's “La Traviata” got me hooked on grand opera. It was my first, performed at 10 a.m. in the university's vast, non-air-conditioned Quonset-hut auditorium. Visual arts, however, remained scarce. The only painting I remember seeing on campus was Vicente Manansala's mural in the first-floor lobby of the LA Building. Sculpture consisted of Guillermo Tolentino's “Oblation” in front of the Administration Building and plaster casts of classical Greek and Roman statues displayed, in figleafed glory, in the Main Library’s third-floor lobby. Once, I went to the National Museum, then housed in the old Bureau of Science Building on Herran Street, and left disappointed that it had neither paintings nor dinosaurs. The newspapers of the day devoted space to music and art criticism. I vaguely remember a reviewer named Morli Dharam describing a concert piece as being in the "French idiom," which prompted music lover Cecilia Locsin to dispatch a Letter to the Editor declaring that Dharam was writing nonsense. Movies cost ₱1.20, and I went to a lot. Films such as “The Great Caruso,” “The Student Prince,” “Brigadoon,” and “Singin’ in the Rain” were additional exposures to grand and light opera. Television had not yet arrived, but I listened faithfully to an hour of classical music aired by DZRH every afternoon at 4 p.m. I once went to a vaudeville show at the Clover Theater near the Santa Cruz Bridge. Once was enough. Live performances were rare in postwar Manila. There simply were not enough venues. The Metropolitan Theater had been badly damaged during the Battle of Manila and was apparently in shape only for burlesque shows and boxing matches. Fortunately, Far Eastern University maintained an active cultural program. I had no problem going out alone, and there I saw, among others, Bizet's “Carmen” performed in Tagalog, with Salvacion Oppus Yniguez terrific as Micaela; “Pagliacci” starring Italian tenor Arrigo Pola (one of Luciano Pavarotti’s teachers); a performance of “The Nutcracker Suite”; and the French film “Jeux Interdits,” whose theme still lingers in my mind. I am no singer, but I was in a UP chorus performance of Handel's “Hallelujah” chorus with First Lady Luz Magsaysay in the audience. Performances were held at unexpected places. I watched Severino Montano's “The Love of Leonor Rivera,” my first experience of theater-in-the-round, at the reception room of Normal Hall, a ladies’ dorm that was otherwise occupied by shy Normal School students and their dashing admirers. Then there was Nick Joaquin's “A Portrait of the Artist as Filipino” performed at Aurora Gardens, an Intramuros ravelin that was part of a prewar tennis complex and that today houses Escuela Taller de Filipinas. University of Sto. Tomas and Sta. Scholastica undoubtedly staged worthwhile productions, but if they did, I never heard about them. Eventually, the Philam Life Auditorium on Isaac Peral Street emerged as Manila's premier concert and theater venue. Then, in 1959, everything changed. I left for the US for graduate studies, first in industrial management and later in finance. New York was an entirely new cultural world. I could afford a few shows at the Metropolitan Opera and Carnegie Hall, admire masterpieces at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and medieval treasures at The Cloisters. Broadway remained beyond my budget, but the Rockettes at Rockefeller Center made up for it. Clearly, my education in the arts was never systematic. What seemed ordinary then became, in hindsight, a pretty good cultural education—one shaped not by abundance but by making the most of whatever opportunities postwar Manila happened to offer. Times are now different. The opening of the CCP in 1969 inaugurated a new phase in Philippine cultural life. It has had its ups and downs over the succeeding decades, and 50 years later, Filipinos and expats alike can have their pick of events such as those announced in “Backstage Pass.” The CCP's main building itself, half a century old, no longer complies with the Building Code, no longer the world-class venue it once was. Renovation began in 2020, and by next year, it will once again be the showcase of the best in Filipino artist creativity and talent. Note: In the field of culture and the arts, your columnist is Chairman of the Cultural Center of the Philippines and serves on the Boards of other museums and cultural organizations. Comments are cordially invited, addressed to walangwala888@gmail.com

Painting the other half. Known for his sweeping, larger-than-life monuments scattered across the southern landscape, from the giant durian at the Davao International Airport to the sacred forms at Tagum’s Christ the King Church, Kublai Millan is no stranger to scale. Yet, in his latest solo exhibition, "Other Half," on view at Art Lounge Manila in The Podium until Aug. 13, the Mindanaoan master pivots from public grandiosity to intimate, painted reflections. To experience Kublai Millan's work is to immerse oneself in the rich culture of Mindanao. His visual language is rooted deeply in the land, its traditions, and the heritage of its indigenous peoples. "I want my works to feel distinctly Mindanaoan," Kublai shares. "The colors of our harvest, the joy of our celebrations, evoke the deep gratitude to the land and its long relationship with its people. I wish my work would represent our culture down south." Looking closely at his canvases, two main motifs consistently anchor his visual narrative: the organic curvy linear and the grounded geometric, both echoing traditional weaves and attire. "The curvy linear represents nature's growth toward the sun, the rivers flow toward the ocean, and all living things within, while the geometrics represents the hard stones and the rugged mountains transformed for millions of years under the stars," the artist says. While art lovers recognize Kublai as a sculptor, shifting to two-dimensional canvases provided a crucial therapeutic reset for the artist. "I am mainly a sculptor building large monuments," he explains. "Due to public demand where collectors could not bring my work home, this led me back to my first love, which is painting. The difficulty of my monuments is the direct contrast of the effortless process of painting. I think I deserved that little break.” While his monuments serve civic history, his current exhibit turns inward, capturing personal history on canvas. Twenty years in the making, "Other Half" serves as a milestone for Kublai, his a visual love letter honoring a two-decade journey alongside his partner, reflecting on love, gratitude, resilience, and the unseen forces that shape our lives. "They are based on personal experiences, putting into canvas my 20-year relationship," Kublai reveals. "I'm taking this chance to express my deep gratitude for a life I enjoyed and shared with another. I have already shared my story, but that is only half of it. This series is the other half." Rather than relying on a single anchor work, Kublai treats the collection as interconnected, where no single piece stands above the rest. "They are all parts of a puzzle, connected to a big whole." Throughout the collection, viewers will notice recurring visual elements, such as red tones balanced with blue, green, and yellow, as well as the recurring presence of the moon. Symbolizing his search for meaning through uncertain times and the patience required for wisdom to unfold, Kublai describes this period as his "moon phase,” reflecting the changing light across years of searching. Throughout the exhibit, Kublai hopes visitors leave with a renewed urgency to cherish those around them. "I wish to invite my viewers to speak their hearts and minds while we still can—time is a gift," he reflects. "Express your gratitude to those who have touched and changed your life." Meanwhile, inside Kublai’s creative workspace is a beautiful chaos. His process is an ongoing cycle of reflection, documentation, and continuous creation. "Every year, I compound my most compelling thoughts and turn them into a series of works. This way, I get to document my growth as an artist and a human being." Knowing when a piece is complete isn't a matter of rigid strategy, but rather an intuitive feeling, guided by physical instinct and subconscious imagery. "I stop when it feels right. My hands would know. But sometimes my dreams speak in riddles and some works would ask for more attention and detail, affection and reflection,” he muses. Surrounded by unfinished ideas and waiting canvases, Kublai embraces the kinetic energy of his workspace. "My studio is hell to the untamed. Piled-up canvases, notes tucked for interpretation. Paints calling to be used. Thoughts become canvases, and each work demands time. It’s a beautiful mess, but I know in time each piece will find its way to an exhibition and to an owner. Then and there, the connection becomes heavenly," he ends. "Other Half" by Kublai Millan runs until Aug. 13 at Art Lounge Manila in The Podium, Mandaluyong City.

PH booters out of semis contention with 0-1 loss to Malaysia. The Philippine national men’s football team was booted out of semifinal contention after yielding a 0-1 loss to host Malaysia in the group stage of the 2026 ASEAN Championship (Hyundai Cup) at the Kuala Lumpur Football Stadium Saturday, Aug. 8. Heading into the contest with hopes of bolstering their semis bid, the Nationals went in with an inspired showing as they attempted to seize the lead early. However, they were dealt a bad surprise when Malaysia breached the Filipino booters’ defense after Pavithran Gunalan found the back of the net in the 16th minute. In the next three minutes, the Philippines almost had an immediate opportunity for a counter and level the game but Javier Gayoso’s header from a pass by Kenji Nishioka didn't go through. With its loss, the squad, mentored by Carles Cuadrat, kissed its semis bid goodbye after reaching the said round in the previous installment two years ago. It was also a semifinalist in the 2010, 2012, 2014, and 2018 editions. Malaysia, for its part, booked its semis spot and will face reigning champion Vietnam. The other Final Four pairing features Singapore and Thailand. The Philippines concluded its campaign with one win – which came from its 4-1 demolition of Laos – and three defeats at fourth in Group B, just ahead of winless Lao squad (0-4). Myanmar (2-2) also got eliminated. The Filipino booters will now turn their attention to the Aichi-Nagoya 20th Asian Games in Japan and this year’s FIFA ASEAN Cup hosted by Indonesia. Both tournaments are scheduled this September.

Rizal rallies past Voyagers, revs up South playoff drive. The Rizal XentroMall Golden Coolers turned hot in the third quarter and bested the Pasay Voyagers, 67-61, on Saturday, Aug. 8, to rev up their playoff drive in the SportsPlus MPBL (Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League) 2026 Season at The Capital Arena in Ilagan, Isabela. Trailing, 27-38, at halftime, the Golden Coolers blitzed the Voyagers, 22-3, in the third quarter to seize control at 50-40 en route to their 13th win against 7 losses in the round-robin elimination phase of the two-division, 26-team tournament. Rizal is in 6th spot in the South division and is on track to advance to the quarterfinal playoffs. Jolo Mendoza and Billy Robles presided over that Rizal scoring spurt that sent the Voyagers down to 11-10. Mendoza, a former member of Batang Gilas, finished with 18 points, spiked by three triples, and 5 rebounds to clinch the SportsPlus best player honors. Alwyn Alday supported Mendoza with 9 points and 2 rebounds, followed by Robles with 7 points, 12 rebounds, 2 assists and 2 blocks, including a crucial block off a driving Lennard Santiago in the dying seconds. Rizal coach Don Dulay said he wants "to build a defensive culture for the Golden Coolers," adding that he's focusing on overall improvement and building camaraderie among the players. Pasay drew 15 points and 13 rebounds from Christian Fajarito, 11 points and 3 rebounds from Renz Alcoriza, and 10 points plus 3 rebounds from Santiago. Fajarito joined the MPBL 1,000-point club and was rewarded with the ball he used to reach the plateau by Commissioner Emmer Oreta. The tournament returns to the Paco Arena on Monday, featuring games between Paranaque and Binan at 3 p.m., Marikina and Mindoro at 5 p.m., and host Manila and San Juan at 7 p.m.

Park Central Towers: Ayala Land Premier’s new chapter in luxury living. Luxury has long been associated with prime addresses, exceptional architecture, and impeccable craftsmanship. But today, the conversation has evolved. Beyond beautiful homes, discerning homeowners are increasingly looking for residences that enrich everyday life with places where wellness, culture, hospitality, and thoughtful design come together to create an experience that extends far beyond the front door. That shift is immediately felt at Park Central Towers, Ayala Land Premier's new luxury development at the corner of Paseo de Roxas and Makati Avenue. Walking into the property, it almost feels as though the pace of Makati slows down. Despite being in the heart of the country's premier financial district, the development offers a remarkable sense of calm. Rich textures, curated interiors, fresh signature scents reminiscent of luxury hotels, and carefully selected artworks create a sensory experience that feels deliberate rather than excessive. Every detail, from what residents see and hear to what they touch, has been designed to elevate daily living. For Ayala Land Premier, this philosophy is a natural extension of more than three decades of creating some of the country's most coveted residential addresses. The company has long believed that the value of a home lies not only within its walls but also in the community, environment, and experiences that surround it. Park Central Towers embodies that vision through three defining pillars: the luxury of location, the luxury of space, and the luxury of choice. At the heart of the city Few addresses in Metro Manila command the prestige of Roxas Triangle. Located at the intersection of Makati Avenue and Paseo de Roxas, Park Central Towers places residents within walking distance of Greenbelt, Glorietta, Ayala Triangle Gardens, premier office towers, restaurants, hotels, and cultural destinations. Yet despite this accessibility, the residential arrival remains intentionally private, with separate entrances that create a clear distinction between residents and visitors to the retail podium. The location also reflects Ayala Land's long-term vision for Makati. Viewed from above, Roxas Triangle and Ayala Triangle form an almost continuous figure-eight or infinity symbol—a subtle representation of the company's master-planned approach to urban development. While Ayala Triangle evolved primarily into the city's commercial and office center, Roxas Triangle was envisioned as its residential counterpart, creating a balanced district where people can live, work, and unwind within a highly connected neighborhood. "People still value exceptional architecture and craftsmanship, but increasingly they're also looking at what life feels like after they move in.
